Before the Orders of the Day are proceeded with, I am obliged to call the attention of. the government once more to the state of affairs that exists in Cote St. Paul in regard to the bridge over the Lachine canal. The superstructure is not being proceeded with, or, at any rate, is not being proceeded with with the expedition which, it seems to me, the government should have the right to exact from the contractor, and the public are suffering very great inconvenience indeed from the delay in the execution of the work. I understand that the contractors have many buildings under way in the city of Montreal, but it must be evident that it will cause greater inconvenience to the public to have this bridge neglected than to have delay in the construction of buildings. There is not in the contract, as I am informed, any clause providing a penalty in case the required works are not finished within a specified

time ; and, probably, tbe contractors, who have this clause In most contracts, are availing themselves of the absence of it in the contract for this bridge. Under these circumstances, and in view of the number of letters of protest that I am receiving every day from people in the locality, I would suggest to the government the advisability of serving the contractors with a protest. If they were served with a formal protest, it would undoubtedly have the effect of hurrying up the work somewhat.

speechtext: I know that the matter has been brought to the attention of the department. But I will call the attention of the minister to the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Monk).

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I wish to call the attention of the government to some speeches that have been made by our High Commissioner in London, Lord Strathcona. A few weeks ago attention was called in the Senate to a speech by Mr. Preston, Commissioner of Immigration, in which he had expressed some opinions which were not thought to be in conformity with the imperialist gospel. To the question asked in the Senate, the Secretary of State replied- very properly, I think-that the government were in no way responsible for the utterances of Mr. Preston, and did not wish to be understood as siding with one party or another in England. Lord Strathcona. speaking on the 14th of May, expressed himself very strongly-as he has done on previous occasions-in favour of the policy of discrimination on the part of England as between the colonies and foreign countries. On previous occasions the noble lord advocated the idea of creating an imperial council. Of course, I have the greatest respect for Lord Strathcona and for his personal opinions on British or imperial politics, but it seems to me rather improper that the official representative of Canada should be understood as taking an active part in British politics and as siding with one or other of the political parties in England. I think it is also undesirable that it should be understood that such utterances are endorsed by the Canadian government, or are meant to express the opinion of the Canadian cabinet. I suppose that when the Canadian cabinet has an opinion to express it must express it in Canada and under its responsibility to the parliament of Canada. It seems to me that some declaration might be made as to Lord Strath cona's speeches similar to that which has been 4nade in the upper House with regard to the speeches of Mr. Preston.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My colleague the Secretary of State speaking in the other
House expressed the view that the government is not responsible for any acts or words spoken by any of its officers if they do not act in their official capacity. Lord Strathcona, we are all glad to know, occupies, in addition to his position as High Commissioner for Canada, a very high position in the social and political world of Great Britain. He has expressed his views on many occasions on different subjects, but I am bound to say, in justice to him, that I am not aware that he has ever on such occasions presumed^ to speak on behalf of the Canadian government. He simply expressed his views and of course he has a right to his own opfnions, but in so doing he does not in any way bind the government of which he is an official.

I desire to draw the attention of the Minister of Militia and Defence to a matter which at the present moment is of considerable importance to many people in this country. The various volunteer corps will soon be called upon to go into camp, and amongst those who are in charge of the work of securing men to increase the force there must be a considerable degree of uncertainty as to what the pay will be for those going into camp. speechtext:
Long service and good conduct pay shall be issued to warrant officers, non-commissioned officers and private soldiers of the active militia, permanent corps excepted, at rates, and under conditions, as hereunder :-
1.	Rates of pay.-1st year, 20 cents ; 2nd year, 40 cents ; 3rd year and afterwards, 50 cents.
2.	Conditions.-
(a.) To have been duly enlisted in a corps of the active militia, other than the permanent corps.
(b.) To have performed for any one annual training, the number of days drill ordered for the corps to which they belong. .
(c.) To have, while performing such drill or training, become reasonably proficient in the duties prescribed for their arm of the service and in the use of the rifle, or the weapon with which they are armed.
(d.) Not to have merited punishment, if a non-commissioned officer, greater than that of a reprimand, or if a private soldier, than that of admonition.
3.	If at any annual training a warrant officer, non-commissioned officer or private fails to comply with the above conditions, he shall forfeit all previous good conduct pay, and shall be entitled only to the net pay of his rank.
4.	Members of corps performing the whole annual training in camp after the first June instant (1904), will be eligible for long service and good conduct pay. Continuous service immediately preceding the date, of the present order may be reckoned to qualify for the higher rates of pay, provided the above mentioned conditions have been fulfilled in connection with said previous service.
From and after the first July, 1904, the provisions of this order shall apply to all corps performing annual training either in camp or at local headquarters.

HUGHES moved for :
Return of the corresp jndonce between Lr. Rutherford, chief veterinary inspector, and Dr. Gerrow, and between the latter and John Campbell, Esq., of Fairview Farm, Mariposa, Wood-ville P.O., in relation to the shipment of sheep to the United States, and the quarantine therein ; as well as in relaiim to the claim made by Mr. Campbell for repayment of express charges connected therew-. h.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the facts substantially are these :	Some time during
the year 1903, Mr. John Campbell, the famous sheep grazer, whose name is well known throughout the length and breadth not only of Canada, but of the United States, and who receives a considerable number of orders from other countries as well for the famous breeds of sheep that he raises, received an order from the prepresident of some breeding institution of Chicago for some sheep to be shipped to Massachusetts. Mr. Campbell, as was his 119
duty, had the animals inspected by the local government inspector, Dr. Gerrow, who communicated with the Department of Agriculture at' Ottawa and received the proper authority for Mr. Campbell to send the sheep to the United States. Mr. Campbell sent them by express, and paid the government officer the inspection fee, and also paid the express charges on the sheep. A short time after they were shipped, the-sheep were returned to Mr. Campbell owing to some technicality that had been overlooked by Dr. Rutherford. I do not know the details of the matter other than these. I am not finding any fault with Dr. Rutherford, but I think that in all fairness Mr. Campbell is entitled to a refund from the government of the expenses to which he has been put through the inadvertence of Dr. Rutherford. I think the minister will agree that Mr. Campbell is certainly entitled to a refund of his dollar inspection fee and his express charges on the sheep. He is willing to let the rest of the expenses go.

I shall be very glad to have the papers brought down. Mr. Campbell applied to the veterinary surgeon, who is authorized to give certificates for export, for a certificate. This veterinary surgeon is not an officer of the department but is authorized to'do this work, and his name was submitted to the American authorities as that of one whose certificates are to be accepted. Mr. Campbell wrote to the department asking about the regulations, not for the New England states, but for the western states, but he alluded to certain regulations with regard to the New England states. Alluding as he did to those regulations, Dr. Rutherford naturally concluded that he knew all about them, and only replied regarding the regulations governing shipments to the western states. Then without further inquiry or communication Mr. Campbell sent his- animals to Massachusetts and they were stopped at the Niagara frontier. As I understand the United States regulations, there is nothing to authorize the stoppage of those animals at the Niagara frontier, but of course that is a matter of interpretation with which we have absolutely nothing to do. But the point of issue is this, that we were not informed that Mr. Campbell was going to send animals to the eastern states. I would have been glad to have paid Mr. Campbell the amount he asked for, but there is no vote in my department out of which I could pay it, and the facts did not warrant my asking parliament for a special item.
There is evidently a misapprehension somewhere. So far as Dr. Gerrow is concerned, is he not an officer of the department appointed by the minister himself ?
He is authorized to give export certificates.
Then is lie not an officer of the department ?
Not in the sense that he is paid a monthly salary.
He is the only veterinary officer of the department who has the power to give a certificate to pass animals in that locality.
He is authorized to do that.

I have here a letter from the deputy minister. While it sums up the matter very plausibly, nevertheless between the lines you can see that even Dr. Gerrow put the case pretty fully fefore the government :
Deputy Minister's Office,
Ottawa, December 7, 1903.
Sir,-I have the honour, by direction, to acknowledge the receipt of your further letter of the 24th November ultimo, with reference to your claim for a refund of express charges on a shipment of sheep to Massachusetts, which you base on the ground that the expense was incurred in consequence of incorrect or insufficient information furnished by the Chief Veterinary Inspector, Dr. Rutherford.
Under date the 16th December last, W. J. Gerrow, V.S., of your town, wrote the Chief Veterinary Inspector that owing to the prevalence in the New England states of foot and mouth disease, there seemed to be some uncertainty among shippers in his locality as to whether there were restrictions on the shipping of animals to the western states and other points. As this letter stated that the writer was aware of the prevalence of the disease in New England, the Chief Veterinary Inspector reasonably assumed that he knew of its natural consequence, the United States quarantine of that area, particularly as both facts have been simultaneously and widely published in the Dominion ; and that as there was uncertainty in the minds of the shippers as to the western states, it would not be in doubt at all as to the prohibition of entry into the infected area itself.
That is the supposition merely of this officer, and there is nothing in the correspondence to show that any such statement was made. Then he proceeds to say :
Dr. Rutherford consequently treated the letter as an inquiry as to the western states.
What was his authority for so doing ? I do not find it here.
And other points in the United States outside of the infected area, and gave the information accordingly.
Here Is the most interesting part of the whole letter :
The term ' United States ' used in his letter of the 20th December last, in referring to Dr. Gerrow's letter, is clearly a typographical error.
How could Mr. Campbell be assumed to know that Dr. Rutherford had made a typographical error in telling him he could ship his sheep to the United States.
Dr. Gerrow asked regarding the western states and not the eastern states. Here is his letter dated December 10th. 1902-the letter to which that letter of Dr. Rutherford was the answer :
The sheep were shipped only in January, 1903.

Yes, the correspondence ran into 1903, but it began in 1902. Here is Dr. Gerrow's letter :
Dear Sir,-Owing to the prevalence in the New England states of foot and mouth disease in cattle there seems some uncertainty among shippers in this locality as to whether there are restrictions on the shipping of animals to the western states and other points.
I am frequently applied to for certificates for shipping sheep and young cattle for breeding purposes to the United States. Would you kindly inform mcf as to where the above-named animals may or may not he shipped at the present time.
That was taken as a request with regard to the western states. '
Will you please read the answer of Dr. Rutherford ?

Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of December 16th asking for information as to whether there are any restrictions on the shipping of animals to the United States and other points.
That is the point that was taken to be a typographical error. It was written ' western ' states as the request applied to the western states.
I understand that the state of Illinois has issued an order prohibiting the importation of animals from Ontario and Quebec unless accompanied by certificates of health from qualified resident veterinarians. I have, however, received no official notification of this action on the part of the state government of Illinois.
I have communicated with the authorities of the state of Illinois asking them to furnish me with a copy of the reported order. As soon as I receive definite information. I will see that Canadians interested are fully apprised of its nature.	.
It is evident that the answer was altogether in regard to the western states. The letter referred to the action of the state of Illinois through which practically all the shipments to the western states must go.

Let me quote the letter of the deputy minister of agriculture :
The minister regrets that you incurred this expense ; but as there is no fault on the part of the department, he is unable to recommend the payment of the claim.
I trust the minister will see his way clear to laying the papers on the table.
Certainly.

And also that he will see his way clear to pay this claim,

seeing that the expense was incurred through the blunder of his officer. I am not finding especial fault, but, as a matter of fair-play the claim ought to be paid.
I am not sure whether I understood what the minister said as to Dr. Gerrow. Did he say that, though a veterinary officer of the department he was not authorized to give certificates for export ?
No. He is not a regular officer of the department, but he is one of those veterinaries in Canada who have been recognized by the American authorities as qualified to give certificates for export.

He said: Is there any objection to this motion ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There will be no objection to slowing the order to go so far as the number of prisoners is concerned, but I would not like to give the names. I do not think it is in the public interest that a man who happens to be allowed out from the penitentiary on ticket-of-leave should have his name published throughout the country. I would also ask my hon. friend to amend his motion in regard to the reasons for the granting of the ticket-of-leave. Sometimes I have a report from a judge saying that he has condemned a man for two or three years for the purpose of giving an example at the time but the judge may subsequently write to me stating that he thinks that at the end of a year or 14 or 15 months the man should he released. I do not think these reasons should be given.

I think my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick) is rather astray in assuming that I want the names of these released prisoners published ail over the country. I do not know whether he takes that view.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would be an official return and of course would be liable to publication.
Not necessarily.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes, it would he a parliamentary return.

Very often returns are made in a manner which shows they are not for publication. The question that presents itself to my mind is how are we to ascertain the working of the ticket-of-leave system unless we can get this information. I did not ask for the names of the prisoners allowed out on ticket-of-leave; I asked for a return of all prisoners. It is possible perhaps to obtain that without giving their full names.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.

But even if it was necessary in a return brought down to parliament, to give the names and the date of conviction, I find that we are very often obliged, seeking information in the House to obtain the names of parties who would much prefer that their names should toot be brought down to parliament. I see nothing in the prohibition mentioned in Bour-inot's work which would protect these parties

against their names being entered in a report which is not necessarily for publication ; which theoretically in fact is supposed to be private, for communication to the members of parliament only, exactly as everything that takes place here is not supposed to be communicated to the public. Theoretically it is supposed to be brought down for the use of members of parliament.
I do not see how we can get that information unless we get the names of offenders. I think my hon. friend may assume that I have no great desire to have their names published throughout the whole country.
I think we are clearly entitled to know the nature of the offence in each case. In fact that is already published in the reports. It is a matter of tracing that will take a great deal of time and my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) will not- intend for a moment that the members of parliament are obliged to go through all that work when they have an absolute right to obtain the information here. Now as to the reason that is the principal source of information which may enable us to form a judgment as to the adequacy of the causes which induced prisoners being released, members of the House will notice that we do not ask for communication of any reports, confidential or otherwise, from the judge or from the officers of the department. These reports, when marked ' confidential ' my hon. friend the Minister of Justice may claim should not be communicated to parliament. There are precedents for that, but surely if we are to judge of the manner in which the law is being administered we have a right to know the reason for the releases.
That reason is mentioned in the public documents. It may be published in some of the public reports of the department for all I know. My hon. friend is mistaken in supposing that the motion calls for any confidential communication of any kind whatever. If a man has been condemned for an offence probably three or four reports of a confidential nature have passed before the ticket-of-leave has been granted him. We do not ask for those. All we ask to know is the reason. Surely we are entitled to know. Was it ill health ? Was it on the recommendation of outside people or on the report of the judge ? We may not be entitled, although that is a question, to the confidential report of the judge, or a letter or other document of a confidential nature as I find upon examining the reasons given in Bouri-not's work for refusing papers moved for, confidential communications, in some case-, from the officers of the department to the head of the department, but surely the high court of parliament is entitled, when inquiring into the way that this law has been administered, to be given the reasons for the release of this man.

Can my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) suggest any case where a judge Mr. MONK.
has any authority or where it is his duty to make a confidential report ?

I may say in answer to my hon. friend that possibly the report of a judge asked as to the advisability of giving a ticket-of-leave may be considered confidential. It is not necessarily confidential, but I can conceive of a case in which a minister might invoke the plea that it was a confidential communication. In the same manner possibly communications from officers of the department asked to make a special inquiry and to make a confidential report might be so treated. But, there are no state reasons. All we want to know is statistical, the offence, the time of condemnation and the reason for granting of the ticket-of-leave. It seems to me that we are asking for something that the House is entitled to obtain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In view of the statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) I have to say that what he asks for is perfectly reasonable and I am quite prepared to give it. I understood the hon. gentleman to ask for names but I apologize if I have misunderstood him. I shall give the different penitentiaries and the number from each penitentiary.
That would be perfectly satisfactory.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to dabble in this matter further than to say that one can very readily see how it will be possible for a star chamber system to grow up in this country if the fullest opportunity is not allowed to parliament to inquire even into the names of these men. Of course, I do not want to be too hard on a man who is sent to penitentiary. There are a good many men in the penitentiaries of this country who are as honest as some of us who are out of it. I do not think that there should be any hesitancy in giving a return of the names of these men together with all information relating to the circumstances under which tickets-of leave were granted to them. I think the public has a perfect right to know who are the men to whom tickets-of-leave are issued why they are issued and who make the recommendations. The recommendations of a good many judges in this country would require to be very carefully examined into before they would bear very much weight with the citizens. The fullest publicity should be permitted in all these matters. We do not want any star chamber system to grow up in the Dominion of Canada.
Motion agreed to.

On the order being called for :

speechtext: I was not here when the matter was arranged with the Prime Minister.

As it is some weeks since this Bill was read a second time, perhaps it might not be improper for me to discuss shortly, the principle of it. The first amendment is to strike out the word ' or ' and insert the word ' and.' That is because the Act as passed makes it quite lawful for the railway company either to fence their track or protect it. The courts have decided that the fencing of a track consists in the fencing of the right of way ending at the cattle-guards, but that is no protection whatever to the highway. So that when a railway company is only bound to do that, it is not bound to protect the people on the highway at all. If the company should be sued for not protecting the highway, it would simply answer : We are not bound to protect, we are only bound to fence the track, and we have fenced the right of way on each side, and turned the fence into the cattle-guard. Consequently we are not liable, notwithstanding the fact that the people on the highway are not protected against passing trains at all. That is the first amendment I seek to make. The hon. gentleman asks me why I will not strike out the words * fenced or,' so as to bind the companies simply to protect ? My reason is this. Protecting has been decided by the Supreme Court to be such as the commission will order and none other, and I seek to have the Act itself declare what shall constitute protection, so that you will not have to go to the Railway Committee, but will find the definition in the section itself, but of course we'want fencing as well. I want to remind the House of what I said on the second reading. My amendment proposes :
And wherever in a city, town or incorporated village a railway crosses a highway at rail level, the said speed of ten miles an hour shall in no event be exceeded, unless the railway company keeps a watchman at such crossing to warn all persons using the highway of approaching trains.
Unless such an amendment be passed, the Railway Act is absolutely nugatory as re-

gards this matter. In the early sections ol the Act all power is given the Railway Commission to order special protection at any place. This is a general provision requiring that .there shall be some measure of protection at all places. The draughtsman of the Act and its promoters understood and . intended that this section was for the purpose of giving In every case protection of some kind to the wayfarer along the highway, so that it would not be necessary for every little village to have, in every case, to get a special order from the Railway Commission to protect the crossing. Last session the rate of speed was increased from six to ten miles an hour. It was argued by the ex-Minister of Railways, Mr. Blair, that as the exigencies of public travel required now a greater rate of speed, it was not unwise to let that rate be increased, without protection at all, to ten instead of six miles an hour. I want to emphasize the fact that there is in my Act no requirement on the railways at all to put any watchman at a crossing if they keep within ten miles an hour. But the Supreme Court has decided, since the General Railway Act was consolidated and amended last session, that notwithstanding this rate of ten miles an hour-it was six in the case before the coui't, that of McKay vs. the Grand Trunk-because there was no order from the Railway Commission, the company was not negligent in not having watchmen even when the train ran at twenty miles an hour. The plaintiffs in that case succeeded in all the Ontario courts and succeeded in convincing one of the judges of the Supreme Court. Two decided to upset the Ontario decision and agreed on what their judgment should be, but the third agreed to set aside the judgment for another reason entirely. There was accord in the decisions of the provincial courts. Judge McMahon decided for the plaintiffs, and his decision was upheld unanimously by the Court of Appeal. There were five judges of the Ontario courts and one of the Supreme Court, Mr. Justice Girouard, in favour of the plaintiffs, and of the three Supreme Court judges against him. one of them, Mr. Justice Sedgewick, did not decide to maintain the appeal on the same ground at all. Should we not have some protection at every crossing in the thickly settled portions of the country ? That was always contemplated. The object always was that there should be no rate of speed exceeding six miles an hour-now it is ten-without some protection. The words of the old statute were ' unless the track is properly fenced.' The Supreme Court decided that fencing up to the highway and then turning into the cattle-guards was all that was required. But what protection does that give to a man on the highway ? You have the whole highway unprotected, yet the regulations contemplated a rate of speed crossing a highway kept down to six miles an hour. Why not let them run a hundred miles an hour Mr. LANCASTER.
if you are not going to protect the people on the highways 7 You must have some protection to travellers, whether in farm wagons, or buggies, or bicycles, or automobiles, or whether they are children going to school, or people walking to or from their work in the thickly settled portions. Some gentlemen may say : Why the thickly peopled portion 1 Because our law has always recognized this principle. Our parliaments, applying their common sense from time to time to this question, have decided that it is necessary for the safety of individuals that in cities, towns and villages, where, owning to the noises, you cannot hear a train coming, and where the view of it is apt to be obstructed, precautions must be taken to prevent loss of life.
What protection have they now ?

None, under the decision of the Supreme Court. But they may get protection by coming to the Railway Commission and getting a special older with regard to any particular crossing, in any city, town or village. But, special application must be made for a special order with regard to every crossing. What we want is what we understood we had under the law, and what the Court of Appeal of Ontario understood was the law, a general provision applying to all cities, towns and villages that, where other safeguards are not present, the rate of speed shall be kept dowTn. WThat sense is there in having in the statute a provision that they shall not run at more than ten miles an hour unless there is some way to enforce that provision ? It would be far more logical to strike out the whole section as a mere anomaly, unless there is some way to reverse or get over the decision of the Supreme Court. If my amendment passes, a general provision will be made applying to all crossings. Of course, it will still be within the power of the Railway Commission to make special order for any cases in which application is made to them. But, even where special application is not made, the people of every city, town and village will have the protection either of the slowing down of the speed to ten miles an hour or of the presence of a watchman to warn people of the passing of the trains.
But the Railway Commission can limit it to less than ten miles an hour.

I am not taking away from the board any power that they now have. This is a general provision applying to every crossing in a city, town or villagegiving the people the right to have a watchman at a crossing or to have the train pass the crossing at not more than ten miles an hour. It is no hardship to the railway company. If they wish to keep down to ten miles an hour, it will not be necessary for

them to provide a watchman. And, if they wish to run faster they can run as fast as they like, if they keep a watchman there. The expense would probably be $2.50 or $3 a day at each crossing of a railway. That is all that is required, a watchman in the day and a watchman at night. They do not even need to provide one for each side of the track, but merely to have at each crossing at which the trains run faster than ten miles an hour, a man whose business it will be to know when the trains are coming and to warn people who may not hear because of the noises of the town and may not see because of intervening objects.
Can the board rule that it is necessary to put on a watchmanan ?

Yes, they can. The representatives of any. city, town or village can come specially to Ottawa and ask the board to have a watchman appointed for a particular crossing. But what I am asking is, as parliament has provided with regard to all crossings in cities, towns and villages that trains shall not run faster than ten miles an hour unless precautions are taken for safety, that this should be enforced and the company that fails to observe the law be made liable for damages. This will avoid the necessity of making application in every case. For instance, in the town of Grimsby in my county there are two crossings of the Grand Trunk, one overhead and one on the level. The representatives of the town would have to come to Ottawa and ask the Railway Commission for a special order- practically they would have to engage in a law-suit-before they could get with regard to that crossing what this amendment would provide with regard to aid crossings. In Port Dalhousie, there are three or four crossings, one of them very dangerous, while the others are more or less dangerous. The representatives of any village would have to come here and apply to the Railway Commission for an order with regard to each particular crossing. Railways are entitled to make their schedules of time between cities. For instance, the express trains go through between Hamilton and St. Catharines. They are entitled to run at forty-five miles an hour, and do not stop between those cities. They run through Jordan, Beamsville, Grimsby, Stoney Creek and Winona. Two of these are incorporated villages and three are not. Those that are incorporated would be entitled, under this amendment, to have a watchman at the crossing. A year ago last December three people in Grimsby were hurled into eternity as they were returning from church in the evening, being run down by a train running at forty-five miles an hour, the approach of which they could not hear. Those people could have applied to the Railway Commission and got an order limiting the rate of speed, but why should they have done so ? *
The statute, as everybody understands it, provided that the trains should not exceed a certain rate of speed at these crossings- formerly six miles an hour, and, under the amendment of last year, ten miles an hour. But the Supreme Court says that, notwithstanding what the statute says about it, unless you have an order from the Railway Commission you cannot get protection. I do not wish to detain the committee, for I realize that if anything is said in the course of the discussion with which I do not agree I shall have an opportunity to answer. We have spent a great deal of time and have just concluded a railway matter which seems to me not of so much benefit to the country as this. I think we might as well get down to this and try and protect the people's lives a little better.

BORDEN (Halifax), I might say a few words at the same time, and perhaps the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) when he rises, will answer the considerations that I shall bring forward. The difficulty that occurs to me on looking at the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of the Grand Trunk vs. McKay, which will be binding on the provincial courts unless the statute is altered or the decision is overruled by the Privy Council, is this ; so long as the railway company has its track fenced according to the requirements of the Railway Act, it can run through any town or thickly populated village at any speed it may see fit. That seems to be the effect of the' decision. The question arises what is proper fencing of the track, and the Supreme Court of Canada decided that it is duly fenced if there is a fence along the line of adjoining properties and if the fence is turned into the cattle guards in the manner prescribed by the statute. That being so, it does not seem that the restriction provided in section 227 of the Act of last year is of much value. In the case of the Grand Trunk vs. McKay, which is reported in XXXIV., Supreme Court of Canada, page 81, the findings of the jury were :
1st. Was the whistle blown before reaching the main street crossing, and if so, at what distance from the crossing was it first sounded ?
A. Yes, at the whistling post.
2nd. If the bell was rung, where did it first commence to ring, and was it ringing continuously or at short intervals until the engine crossed the street -where the accident happened?
A. Bell starte_d to ring east of Main street eight or ten rods, and rang continuously.
3rd. Is the Main street crossing at Forest in a thickly peopled portion of the village ?
A. Yes.
4th. At what rate of speed was the engine running at the time it crossed Main street ?
A. About twenty miles an hour.
5th. Was such a rate of speed, in your opinion, a dangerous rate of speed for such locality ?
A. Yes.	[DOT]
6th. Was the death of Mrs. McKay and the injury to Joseph McKay caused in consequence

of any neglect or omission of the company ?
If so, what was the neglect or omission, in your opinion, which caused the accident ?

It seems to me that sixteen is altogether too low an age. Certainly, in our part of the country boys are only leaving school at that age and have not had much time to learn the ways of the world and how they should protect themselves in case they are accused. And, even if, as the minister hints, a lad may be a hardened criminal at nineteen or twenty, I cannot see what harm can be done to the state by allowing his parents to advise him. LANCASTER (Lincoln and Niagara) moved second reading of Bill (No. 4) to amend the Act respecting Certificates to Masters and Mates of Ships.

I would ask my hon. friend to suspend the Bill for the present. I am preparing a Bill having in view the consolidation of all the laws concerning the examination of masters and mates. Should it not be ready in time this session, I promise the hon. gentleman that he will have an opportunity of discussing this Bill. I hope to be able to give him that assurance within the course ot this week. This is a very important matter, and I think the hon. gentleman will attain the same end by letting this Bill stand.

I have waited since the beginning of the session for this promised Bill, and I have been urged, in fact warned, by persons interested to push this matter through. I am within the judgment of the majority of this House at all times, but in reply to the Minister ot Marine I would say, that we ought to discuss this Bill now and see how far the government will adopt the principle of it. If this were done, I would get rid of some of the responsibility resting upon me. I undertook .to try to get the law amended on the lines of this Bill, and so far as we can learn from the government they don't object to the amendments here proposed. Seeing that the government is moving to take away Wednesdays and Thursdays from private members, I do not care to take the responsibility of letting the matter stand. From the statement made by the Minister ot Marine there appears to be some doubt whether he will bring his Bill down this session, and the opportunity he promises of discussing this Bill might come at the er.d of the session when some gentlemen who take an interest in the Bill might not be here.
