MACLEAN (East York) moved second reading of Bill (No. 6) to amend the Railway Act, 1903. He said : Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat at a loss how to proceed with the discussion of this Bill. I could get through in a very short time to-night if I had an assurance that fve could go into committee and discuss the Bill clause by clause. The clauses of the Bill are all very different. First of all, I deal with the constitution of the Railway Commission ; then I pass on to the question of telephones, express companies and passenger rates. I would like very much to make an arrangement with the government for a day, so that the House could go into committee and discuss these several amendments. As I cannot get that assurance, I must go on to-,night. The object of the first clause is to bring express companies within the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. They are not within it to-day, and yet these companies are all powerful in the matter of rates.. As a matter of fact, the express companies in this country are owned by the railway companies. The so-called Dominion Express Company is but a donkey-engine of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; the Canadian Express Company holds the same relation to the Grand Trunk Railway I Company ; the Mackenzie and Mann system has also its express company ; !
120$
and yet, as the law stands to-day all these express companies, in the matter of rates and the way they treat the public, are independent of the Railway Commission. The business men of this country think that if the railway companies and their charges and their treatment of the public, are to be subject to the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission, so also should the express companies. The great grievance the public have against the railway companies as to which the Railway Act is supposed to afford them protection, is in the matter of unfair discrimination. The express companies have it in their power to discriminate in such a way as to ruin the business of certain individuals in this country. Everybody knows that the Standard Oil Company became the powerful factor that it is to-day in the com mei-ce of America, because of the unjust dii crimination afforded it by railway companies The same thing can happen on a much smaller scale in a way to affect a great many people, by these express companies giving unfair discrimination. I was looking over a book of railway statistics the other day, when I saw the statement that one of the best assets of the great Vanderbilt railway, the New York Central, was the $3,000,000 of shares which it holds in the American Express Company, giving it control. This shows how powerful these concerns are. Not many years ago when John Wanamaker was postmaster general of the United States, he was asked to introduce a parcel post system similar to what they have in Great Britain and Germany. He said :	' I would like
very much to distinguish myself as a member of this administration' by introducing that sort of a parcel post system in the United States ; but there are four reasons why we cannot have it. ' He was asked what they were. He said : ' The first is the American Express Company, the second is the United States Company, the third is the Southern Express Company, and the fourth is the Wells-Fargo Express Company. ' These companies are so powerful in the United States that they are in a position to prevent the parcel-post system being adopted in that country. They are so powerful that they have prevented a postal note being adopted'in the United States, or a money order system as good as we have here, and they maintain a system much inferior to what exists in England. My proposal simply is to bring the express companies within the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission, so that their charges should be subject to the control of that body, and the public can cite them before the commission and compel them to justify their proceedings. That is a very reasonable proposition. We fought last session to have the express companies covered by that Railway Act, but we were voted down. The boards of trade of this country have asked that the express companies be brought within the jurisdiction of the Act.
Have yon any data as to the amount of business done in the country by the express companies ?
No.

Who says ' no ' ? Probably the gentleman is from the west. Yet it was a western member, and a Liberal, the hon. member for Alberta (Mr Oliver) Who said in this House a few months ago that the people of the west feared above all things that the Bell Telephone monopoly would get the west in its grasp as it already had the east. I do not want to antagonize the Bell Telephone Company. I want those who have their money in it to make a fair return on their investment. But I do not like to see a company with a public franchise treating the public as they are doing. They seem to think that success is to be attained by keeping out rivals, strengthening their monopoly and keeping up rates. But, if they would accommodate the public and lower the rates they would make more friends, and I believe they would make more money for their shareholders.
Now I come to the question of passenger rates. If the Bill goes to the Committee of the Whole House, or, if I have to go to the Railway Committee, I will give to hon. gentlemen every opportunity to deal
Is there legislation in the United States of that character ?

Of the United States ? No, it is state legislation in every case. I do not know whether they apply that to other railways ; if they found the Grand Trunk in this country carrying people for less than 2 cents, they would certainly pass an Act in the United States or in the state legislatures compelling them to give the same rate to Americans.
Here is something worse than that. These railroads that carry people in the United States carry traffic that originates in Michigan and New York at 2 cents alongside of Canadians who have to pay them 3 cents. Is that not an injustice and an unfair treatment of Canadians ?
ROSiS (Ontario). Are you sure of that ?

I am sure of that; and I asked Mr. Kingsmill, the solicitor of the Michigan Central road, to have his passenger traffic expert here, and I would prove it. I have not got him here yet, but I will get him.
What is that ?

I have asked Mr. Kingsmill to have a passenger expert here representing either the New York Central or the Michigan Central before the committee of this House, and I will prove by his own tariffs that they carry people through Canada at 2 cents a mile sitting alongside Canadians, whom they charge 3 cents.

In the committee the statement was made that a passenger from Detroit to Buffalo could get a certain rate, and that he would have to pay from Windsor, just across the river, a much dearer rate to Buffalo. I think I can deny that statement.
Does the hon. gentleman still hold that the statement I made is not correct ?
No ; I never made that statement.
Therefore, it is not correct.

I can, of course, bear my hon. friend out in that. Let me tell you how it works out. Let us suppose that you are in Battle Creek and want to go to St. Thomas, the hon. gentleman's own town. There are so many miles of that trip in the state of Michigan and so many in the province of Ontario. They will sell you a through-ticket between these points and charge you 2 cents a mile in the state of Michigan and charge you 2 '60 cents a mile in Canada, which is four-tenths of a cent less per mile than they would charge the Canadian who buys in Detroit or Windsor. I believe you can buy in Chicago for St. Thomas and probably travel on the Canadian portion of the Michigan Central from Chicago to St. Thomas for 2 cents a mile, but no Canadian who buys his ticket at' Windsor or Detroit, or anywhere within Canada, can get these advantages. Is that fair treatment to Canadians ? Is that fair treatment accorded to Canadians by the Vanderbilt interest, which includes Rockefeller and the Vanderbilts ? It now includes the New York Central, the Michigan Central and thousands of other miles of railway, and they are carrying people all over the United States, especially in Michigan and New York, and carrying them through Canada at 2 cents a mile, but they will not carry Canadians for 2 cents. The same thing is done by the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Wabash, and will be done by the P6ra Marquette, if it can get the running rights it is now seeking. Is it not time that we should compel these great railroad corporations to treat us at least as well as they treat other people. Under these various proposals we can have a general principle applying 2 cents to all railroads. You can have the Michigan law, which is. based on the passenger traffic of the road. It starts at 3 cents and grades down to 2J cents, and has really worked great relief. Or we can have a law that any railway company doing business in Canada and also doing business outside of Canada shall give at least as good passenger rates inside of Canada as outside of it.
ROSiS (Ontario). Are there any states but Michigan and New York that give it ?

Yes, there are quite a number of states where it is effected by competition and one thing and another. I think the greater portion of Ohio is under a 2-cent rate. We have in Canada some legislation in favour of cheaper transportation, and it ought to be made so that it will apply to Ontario and Quebec any way. The Rob-iin government in Manitoba was making a deal with the Mann & Mackenzie system, the Canadian Northern, just like the govern-

eminent to-day are making a deal with the Grand Trunk in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific. They demanded terms. They did not so much demand terms on the new railway as they did on all their system, and here is the little clause in the statutes of! Manitoba of 1901, which reads :
When this agreement takes effect, the company shall reduce Its passenger rates In Manitoba, to not exceeding 3 cents per passenger mile
The little province of Manitoba in that agreement got a three cent per mile passenger rate over the Canadian Northern and the next day the Canadian Pacific Railway came to a three cent per mile passenger rate and gave it to the people of Manitoba The Grand Trunk to-day, on the most populous portion of its line, is charging over three cents. The rate between Toronto and Cobourg is a little over three cents a mile. Between Toronto and Montreal, on that portion of the road which has the largest traffic the Grand Trunk Railway Company is charging over three cents a mile. Granting that the deal with the Grand Trunk Pacific was a good one, and granting that the Grand Trunk Railway was made a party to the agreement as it has been, then I say that the government should have compelled the Grand Trunk Railway Company to have made a maximum passenger rate over the whole of its lines in Canada. It was done in Manitoba and it could have been done by this agreement or it could have been covered by the general Act. But even this is not all. The old government passed an Order in Council in connection with the Intercolonial Railway fixing the passenger tariff and it is scaled for 400 miles first class, at $8 and for 534 miles, second class, at a cent and a third a mile. If the government thought that was a good passenger rate to impose on its own railway in the maritime provinces where there is no congested population, surely the government ought to impose the same passenger rate on the different railways in this country.	.
What effect has that upon the earning power of the railway ?

I think travelling is' much greater in the maritime provinces and I think the maritime members will admit that and that they will be the last to consent to a repeal of that law. It has stimulated travel in the maritime provinces. We have a reduced rate of travel on the government road, we have a provision for a reduced rate in the Manitoba Act and we ought to make provision in our general law to compel outside companies to lower their rates. I pointed out last session that under the original agreement between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the government of Canada the Grand Trunk Railway Company bound itself to give a penny rate per mile, second class, between Toronto and Mr. MACLEAN.
Montreal. It is not carrying out that agreement. I put a question on the paper some time ago asking the government whether the agreement was the same to-day as it originally was and I got an evasive answer. I believe it is still the same and I believe the Grand Trunk Railway Company could be compelled to give that lower service. When it comes to an issue in this House we may take any one of these proposals- a two-cent rate, or the Michigan law, or we can adopt a law that any company doing business in the United States that gives a two-cent rate outside of Canada shall give a two cent rate in Canada, or we can apply the Intercolonial Railway tariff to all railways. The people are entitled to a reduced passenger rate. I have here a book which contains a study of the question of passenger rates in America. I am only going to make the slightest reference to it but I would like any hon. gentleman who is interested in this question to look it up. It is :
Publications of the University of Pennsylvania-Series of Political Economy and Public Law-No. 10-Passenger Traffic of Railways-Walter E. Weyl.
Mr. Weyl made a thorough study of the passenger tariff of the United States and Europe and his conclusions are to the effect that the railways have mot sufficiently known their own interests, that they had to be forced to give reduced rates by the governments of Europe. Wherever these reduced rates were given travel was stimulated and he says that if the American railway managers reduced their rates their profits would be increased. That is the thesis he starts out with aud he makes a strong argument in support of it. There is a movement in the United States to-day and it is a rapidly growing one based on the success of reduced postal charges It is based on the claim that a cent a mile will stimulate travel so that the railways will make more money than ever, that it will promote the trade of the country, increase railway travel and assist in the education of the people. That movement is growing in the United States. A report in favour of it has been printed by congress recently and this report also can be found in the library. That is my argument in support of these changes in the Railway Act and whether we go into the Railway Committee or into the committee of the whole House, I intend to make good every one of the statements I have made here to-night. I have more details and I shall be glad to furnish them. Taking the Bill up clause by clause will give every hon. member an opportunity of being heard on the question and of putting forward his views. I want to have as full a discussion of the matter as possible from all points of view and if the railways want to be heard I will give them every opportunity, but I certainly want the Vanderbilt

interest to understand now that when it comes to' this House asking for legislation, asking for an Act of consolidation, the very words that were put into the statutes of the state of New York as affecting the lines owned and controlled by it to the effect that the passenger rate shall not exceed two cents a mile shall also be applied to it in any legislation that it may desire here. I believe that if it is appealed to on broad public lines the Vanderbilt interest will accept that two cent rate and incorporate it in its private Bill. At any rate the facts have been presented to the House to-night. We can discuss them much more fully on the different clauses of the Bill and any information that I can give on the matter I would be only too glad to supply to kon. gentlemen.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that I am very glad to have an opportunity of supporting in many respects the Bill which the kon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) has moved tonight, but I do not quite agree with the whole of that hon. gentleman's argument. I am very glad to support that feature of it which proposes to bring express companies under the general Act because I believe they ought to be brought under the control of the commission. Now. in respect to the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners on a question of law overruling the other members of the commission, and controlling them in so far as that is concerned, it seems to me to be a little inconsistent in view of the fact that in case of an appeal the appeal is made to the Governor in Council and the composition of that body before whom the appeal is brought may be as a matter of fact laymen. Therefore, the chairman gives a decision affecting a question of law although the appeal is brought before the Railway Committee of the Privy Council for decision.
If it is a question of jurisdiction, that may be referred to the Supreme Court, and the amendment of my hon. friend. (Mr. Maclean) would remove some of the inconsistencies that exist. In my section of the country-the county of Middlesex-a large number of farmers have a telephone system, and they experience a great deal of difficulty In trying to get connection with the Bell Telephone Company lines. The amendment would remove that difficulty. As to the reduction of passenger rate's, I may say that some time ago I had my name attached to a Bill asking for certain legislation in this House, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) took occasion to move an amendment to that Bill asking that a two cent a mile rate should be applied to that particular railway. I opposed that for the reason that I did not think it was a fair course to pursue with respect to any particular railway. If we are going to apply a two
cent rate to the railways of Canada, we should not select a particular line to experiment on, and especially so on that line of railway running through the southwestern portion of Ontario to the eastern states-a road that so far as local traffic in Canada is concerned would not be worth one single dollar if they had to rely on the money they got out of Canada. Another point is, that the Canada Southern Railway never received in any shape of form one dollar of bonus from the Dominion of Canada, while the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Lake Erie and Detroit that are parallel lines, all received bonuses from this government. The Canada Southern Company practically built their line of railway at their own expense, and at all events without any assistance from the Dominion government, and I thought that it would be an injustice to apply such a rule to that company alone. Reference has been made to what occurred in the state of New York in 1861, but the legislature of that state at least had the good taste to legislate with respect to one of its own lines of railway, it was not good taste to single out an American line that passes through our country, a Yankee road, if I may term it. built by money raised in the United States. If the Americans had taken the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Grand Trunk Railway running through the United States and applied a law to them that they declined to apply to their own railways, we in Canada would undoubtedly have taken that as an affront. For that reason I opposed the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) at the time, and thought then as I think now, that it would have been most unfair legislation. I wish to be placed on record as being willing to support any general law which will bring about a reduction of freight and passenger rates: but I shall decline to support any measure that will single out any particular line of railway for the purpose of imposing on that line obligations which we do not impose on others. I do not go so far as to say that every railway in Canada shall be compelled to reduce its rates, because when we look over the records we find that several railroads in this country are not making sufficient to meet their running expenses, and I think it would be improper for us to place such obligations on the investors in those lines of railways who are not getting any return on their investment. For that reason it might be unfair to apply the principle in a general way throughout the country. But if the law is made general in its application to railways which have receipts over and above running expenses, I am willing to support a law that will compel such roads to carry passengers at two cents a mile, if parliament in its wisdom should deem that to be proper legislation. That is all I wish to

say, and I say It in order to make myselt perfectly understood as to where I stand on this particular question.
I would not have said anything on this Bill at the present time, had I known whether it was to be dealt with by the Committee of the Whole or by the Railway Committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Railway Committee.

Then it is my opinion that this Bill could be as intelligently dealt with in this House as in the committee. If it were necessary to get expert evidence that would be a justification to send it to the committee, but we have had analogous questions dealt with in this House over and over again. If the various provisions of the Railway Act itself could be properly dealt with in this House, I do not understand why these proposed amendments which are of a comparatively trivial character, could not also be dealt with in this House. It has been our experience in the past that these Bills are referred to the committee for the purpose of being buried, and I think that will be our experience in the future. If it were not a reflection on the committee, I would be disposed to say that these Bills were sent there for that purpose. When parliament desires to prevent a Bill from becoming law, and yet does not want to leave a record on * Hansard ' of what took place, the Bill is referred to a committee. I wish to say a word as regards the argument advanced by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Ingram) 'as to whv he opposes this Bill.
I don't oppose the Bill.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say that he opposed that feature of the Bill which proposed to put restrictions upon a foreign company running through Canada, and which we did not put on our own railways here.

I wish to say most emphatically that I am in favour of every feature of this Bill. I bad reference to a former Bill with respect to the Canada Southern Railway, aud my reference was entirely apart from this Bill altogether.

My understanding of the hon. gentleman's argument was, that it would be improper to compel a foreign company to carry passengers through Canada at two cents a mile, if we did not compel our own railways to do it. Am I right in that ?

The hon. gentleman is not l'ight in that. This Bill is supposed to be a general law and I am supporting it. The other matter of which I spoke was an incidental reference to a discussion which took place some time ago.

The Grand Trunk Railway is a Canadian railway running in part through the United States, and the United States have legislated with respect to it exactly as the hon. member (Mr. Ingram) says we have no right to legislate with respect to American railways.

I beg to differ from my hon. friend. The legislation in Michigan applies to the Michigan Central, the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific Railway and every other line irrespective of whether they are American or Canadian.

This law applied to the Grand Trunk Railway in the state of Michigan, and it did not apply to several of their own railways. It was meant to apply to the Grand Trunk, and the Grand Trunk was a Canadian road. If the people of Michigan did that with a Canadian railway, is it not equally just for the people of Canada to do the same with the Michigan Central Railway when it comes through Canada ?

I wish to draw the hon. gentleman's attention to this fact, that there was no distinction made between the rates. If a railway had a certain revenue, the law applied to it, whether it was the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific or the Michigan Central. But, in this case, whatever the ra-venue is, you are applying the rate to the Michigan Central and not to the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific.
We are only proposing to do with regard to the Michigan Central what the state of New York has done. It imposes a special condition on the New York Central, and on the New York Central alone.
Certainly, in their own country.

Can there be any injustice in applying the same law to the Michigan Central in Canada, that the state of Michigan has applied to it in Michigan-that is, that when the earnings of the railway reach so much per mile, they shall give a two-cent rate, the earnings of the railway in Canada are up to what they are in the United States when it is compelled to give the two-cent rate ; then are we asking anything unjust when we ask that it shall do for the Canadian people what it does for the Michigan people ? If the proposal were to establish a two-cent rate all over Canada, I frankly admit that I would not be in favour of it, because there are localities where the earnings of the railway are not such as to justify such a reduction. But I am in favour of the two-cent rate in the thickly settled portions of Ontario. Let me state by way of illustration what occurred at one time on the Grand Trunk Railway. I took the train at Grand Rapids in Michigan, where two young men got on board with their bicycles. These were carried as baggage, and the young men were given checks for them. But

as soon as the train reached the Canadian line, the bicycles were put off, and the young men had to pay either 75 cents or $1.75 on each bicycle to Toronto. We were travelling on a railway which had been heavily subsidized jn Canada, and not subsidized in the United States, and yet it gave better advantages in the United States, where it was not subsidized, than in Canada, where it was subsidized so largely. The same thing applies to this railway. On the Michigan part of it, which was not subsidized, you can travel at two cents a mile, but as soon as you reach Canada where it has been subsidized, you pay nearly three cents a mile. If either should receive special consideration at the hands of the railway, it should be the Canadian people and not the Michigan people.
With regard to the provision of the Bill relating to telephones, I am inclined to believe it one of the greatest absurdities of the day, whether parliament intended it or not, that companies which are really common carriers are allowed to discriminate in favour of one who uses the Bell Telephone as against another who uses another telephone. Go into any part of the country where there are private telephone lines, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company vyill not allow them to have connection with any of its offices, while it gives the Bell Telephone Company a monopoly. Our law provides for equal justice to all, and that there shall be no discrimination in favour of one as against another ; but we are allowing such a discrimination to-day, and the sooner we remedy it the better.
With regard to that feature of the law which gives the chairman of the Railway Commission the right to decide questions of law without any appeal, as against the two other members of the commission, giving the minority the control over the majority, it seems to me to be unorthodox, to say the least. If there were any other court in Canada which gave its decisions in a similar way, it would be the laughing stock of the world. Whether that provision was put in the law designedly, so that the chairman of the commission should be able to take advantage of it, or accidentally, I do not know. Knowing his relation to telephone companies in this country, I rather think it was designed by the government, and that they were all aware how it would work out. If that be so, I will leave them to settle that matter with the electors of the country. When it becomes known that the government inserted that provision for that purpose, I tell them that they will have a public sentiment to deal with more powerful than they have calculated up to the present time. The sooner we amend that part of the law, the better for our own credit.
With regard to the clause of the Bill providing that the Railway Act shall apply to express companies as well as railway companies, I have always held strongly the opinion that it should. Express companies are controlled by the railway companies, and a large part of the traffic is that carried by the express companies.
. Mr. FITZPATRICK. If I were to express my own personal view of this Bill, I would ask the House now to reject the measure for the following reasons. In the first place the first clause deals with the question of express companies, but during last session, alter a full discussion on this subject, it was decided that the provisions regarding express companies should not form part of the Railway Act. Having come to that conclusion last year, and in view of the fact that the Act itself has not been in operation a year now, it would be improvident for us to adopt the proposed amendment at present. I would also like to draw attention to the fact that if it were intended to give the commission control of the rates of express companies, it would be necessary to have very much more ample provisions than those contained in the Bill. In the Act many of the provisions for controlling freight rates are inapplicable to express companies, and it would be necessary to insert several clauses in the Bill in order to give the commission control of express companies. My hon. friend also proposes that there should be an amendment of section 10 of the law, which gives the chairman of the commission the decision of questions of law. My hon. friend must bear in mind that two of the commissioners form a quorum under the Railway Act, and if so, there must be some controlling power to determine the question submitted. But in addition he must remember that section 10 of the Railway Act provides that the commissioners must unanimously decide that the question is a question of law before the interpretation of that question is left with the chief commissioner. My hon. friend deals in section 3 with the question of compensation to telephone companies. It would be improper for us to pass this legislature at present, because that question is now under consideration by the Supreme Court on a reference of the chairman.

What is the reference?
Mr. FITZPATRICK-with reference to the measure of damage to be allowed in a case, I think, from the county of York. That question has been referred to the Supreme Court, and until we have the decision of that court it would be imprudent to lay down a rule by which damages should be fixed. With respect to the two cent rate, that is a very large question, which interests railway companies, and should not be decided without our having the proper statistics before us. My hon. friend himself, a short time ago, when this matter was up before the House on a

previous occasion, suggested the propriety of having fuller information ; and in view of that suggestion, I would ask this Bill to he referred to the Railway Commission so that we may have the opportunity of considering the question of a two cent rate more fully and of getting more information on that point.

1 do not intend to discuss the merits of the Bill at any length, hut for the reasons I gave last year on the General Railway Bill, 1 think that the first amendment proposed is in the public interest, and ought to carry. If this amendment be not in the public interest, then neither is the General Railway Act we passed last session. Although I do not wish to admit personally that the Railway Commission has proved a success, still if there is any sense in establishing it, there is none in excluding express rates from its jurisdiction. We know that under the excuse. of carrying goods by express the railway companies will be able practically to defeat the law and perpetrate a frauu on the country. As regaids the second clause, I do not see at present how we can very well reject this amendment without placing altogether too much power in the hands of the chief commissioner. .All that the commissioners have to do is to decide that a certain question is a question of law and then the chief commissioner has the sole decision. X am further of opinion that there can he no appeal from his decision, for the appeal to the Privy Council can only be had from the decision of the commissioners acting as a body, and dealing with matters that are not questions of jurisdiction only. If we do not adopt this amendment, we leave it in the power of one commissioner to decide any question which the two others may say is a question of law. I understood the Minister of Justice to contend that the commissioners must unanimously decide that the question is one of law before it can be referred to the chief commissioner. I do not thus read the section. There is nothing to say that the decision of the commissioners must be unanimous. Two of them may decide that a certain question is one of law and then the chief commissioner has the sole power. We might thus find ourselves reduced to this position. One of the commissioners might be clearly of opinion that the question is not a question of law and another may be of opinion that it is. You will therefore have practically a division 'of opinion, and in such a case the chief commissioner could by agreeing with one other obtain for himself the absolute disposal of the question without any appeal, because, with all deference, I submit to the Minister of Justice that section 44 does not provide an appeal from the decision of the chief commissioner on a question of law, and that is the only section which covers the question of appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In questions which are not questions of law there is an appeal to the Governor in Council. As to section 3, I do not dissent from the view taken by the Minister of Justice, namely, that it might be well to wait for the decision of the Supreme Court and I submit to my hon. friend from East York that after we get a decision from that court, we may be able to amend the law much more satisfactorily than we could do at present. As regards the two cent passenger rate, I do not see any excuse whatever for sending that question to the Railway Committee. Of course my position on these public Bills is pretty well known by this time in the House, and I am still of the opinion that all public measures should lie dealt with in the Committee of the Whole House once and for all. The fact that they are public Bills, and not measures of private legislation, is the reason why the House should deal with them. When they are sent to the committee, no progress is made, for nobody is bound by the decision of that committee. They have to come back here to be dealt with even if the committee should report against them.
Even if it reports that absolutely nothing could be done with the Bill, still it must come back to this House. We are not bound by the report of the committee, and we must solemnly sit here and deal with the question again. This seems to me a waste of time. And, as the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) said this evening, and as has been said by more than one of us on more than one occasion, it seems a mere excuse for disposing of the Bill without dealing with it on its merits, avoiding the responsibility of killing it, though the intention is that it shall l>e killed. In Committee of the Whole we can deal with this question of 2-cent passenger rate much better than in the Railway Committee. What information can we get in the Railway Committee that we hav? not here V We are not going to ask our constituents down to tell the Railway Committee how to vote. Yet they are the only ones we have to consider. We are here to make laws for the good of the people. We need no railway expert to tell us that, in this stage of railway development, in this period of the history of Canada, it is fair or it is unfair to propose a 2-cent maximum rate for passenger travel. If there are reasons why that rate should not be adopted, those reasons can be known to us now. If we do not know them we are to blame, for we should have been able to find out before now what the wishes of our constituents are with regard to the matter. I have no doubt whatever that the large majority of the people of Canada-certainly of the part of Canada I represent-are clearly in favour of saying that the time has arrived when the railways of Canada should be restricted to a maximum passenger rate of 2 cents a mile. I think the purpose of this amendment is sometimes misunderstood-not necessarily in

this House, but outside of it. Some seem to assume that the proposal is to make a rate of 2 cents per mile, no more or no less. But the amendment of the hon. member for Bast York (Mr. Maclean) proposes a maximum rate, still leaving it to the Railway Commission to say, if they wish, that the rate shall be II cents or 1 9-10 cents.
No.

The hon. gentleman says 'no.' But if he will read the Railway Act of last session carefully-or, for that matter, even if he will read it carelessly-he will find that the Railway Commission have the power to fix the rates, and this amend-, ment does not take from them that power This merely provides that they shall not make a rate of more than 2 cents per mile.
And I believe that the majority of the people of Canada are in favour of such an enactment. 1 support it because it is in the interest of the country, because it is time the railways had this much restriction put upon
them,	and because this should be given to guide the Railway Commission. For the Railway Commission know what we do here.
If we reject this amendment they will take it as a hint that the representatives of the , people of Canada-representing the people more directly than the Railway Commission does-believe that a rate of 2 cents per mile is not sufficient, and they may be deterred from imposing that rate, even though they may think' it fair. At all events, we in this House, representing the people, ought to tak# the responsibility, nor should we shirk it in the least by .referring it to the Railway ,
Committee or anybody else. Personally, I am in favour of the proposition, and will support it with vote and voice until otherwise advised by my constituents-which, X feel sure, will never occur for some time.

When the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) last session moved a resolution in this House in favour of a passenger rate of 2 cents a mile on the railway I supported it, 1 and I feel like supporting the Bill that he has now introduced. I do not need to speak ' at length upon the subject just now, because it will be brought up either in the Committee of the Whole or in the -Railway Committee, and I shall have an opportunity of speaking
then.	It has been incidentally remarked here that the Canada Southern, or rather the Michigan Central, a railway which runs through my constituency, has been singled out as the first to-have imposed upon it this rate of 2 cents per mile. This Bill says nothing about the Michigan Central in particular, as I understand it, but simply provides that all railroads shall carry passengers for not more than 2 cents per mile.
There may be some force in the argument of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that in the sparsely settled dis- _ tricts it would not pay to carry passengers 1 egraph lines.
for 2 cents per mile. AYhether that is true or not, I am satisfied that in the older sections it will be a benefit, not only to the people of the country, but to the railways themselves to have a 2-cent rate. For it has been shown that even when they cut rates themselves, or when they carry people at excursion rates, they make more money than in the ordinary way. If that be true, we are legislating in their interest when we make a 2-cents rate for the railways. It has been complained that the Michigan Central has been singled out. But the reason it has been singled out by a proposal made some time ago in the Railway Committee was that the company were asking for legislative favours from this parliament, and it was thought to be time for us to reciprocate and get some favours from them. It has been said that the Michigan Central was an American railway. But the charter was granted to Canadians. The Canada Southern people ran the road for a number of years, but having no connection with the east and west they could not make it pay, and they leased the road to the New York Central and the Michigan Central for a term of years, and now I understand they released it for 999 years. We find that this Michigan Central road is carrying American passengers for 225 miles across southern Ontario at the rate of 2 cents a mile. But if a man buys his ticket, say in Windsor, and rides to Fort Erie, he must pay 3 cents a mile. And it is very humiliating to a Canadian to sit in a seat alongside an American who rides at 2 cents a mile, while the Canadian himself has to pay 3 cents. If the road is compelled to carry passengers at 2 cents a mile, either they will do all the passenger business or the other roads serving the same territory will have to reduce their rates to the same level. The county I have the honour to represent gave this Canada Southern road $225,000 as a bonus. They paid interest on that money for twenty years, and I think we are entitled to some of the favours if nothing else. Of course, I admit that the railroad has been a great benefit, as all railroads are. We could not very well exist in Canada without railroads, but that does not say that the railroads should own the country. They should give us some privileges as we give privileges to them. Here is an opportunity for us, and if we let this escape and do not now compel these people to give us a 2-cent rate, then we are derelict in our duty, and we ought not to represent the people of this country, if we neglect this opportunity.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.	.
Hon. CHARLES FITZrATRICK (Minister of Justice) moved :
That the Bill be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Tel-

I am not satisfied that this Bill should go to the Railway Committee without a reason being given for it. On the motion which has just been made I intend to refer to one or two things which have been said during the debate. If we adopt the Michigan law which compels railroads earning over $3,000 a mile, the Michigan Central which now earns over $3,000 would have to give a two cent a mile rate in Canada.
They earn $1,000 a mile on the Canada Southern.

No, the Canada Southern is not earning $4,000 a mile, but it earns over $3,000 a mile. The Grand Trunk today earns over $2,200. The earnings of the Canadian Pacific Railway are coming up very rapidly and are between $1,700 and $1,800 a mile.

About $1,500.
Sir. S1ACLEAN. No, it is nearly $1,700, I think. And so the Slichigan law would seem to be the one which ought to be aj>
plied in this country. It catches the roads that make a lot of money, and makes them give a lower rate.
Does the road that gives a two cent rate pay ?

All the shareholders have a guaranteed income for 999 years of 21- or 3 per cent a year. They are well satisfied and the New York Central is well satisfied because they make good money out of using the Canada Southern for through traffic.
In reference to sending this Bill to the Railway Committee, I would say that I had a Telephone Bill in this House dealing with the general question of telephones, and I was sent to the Railway Committee with it. Let me read to the House the opinion of the Slunicipal Union in regard to that. The Slunicipal Union, I wish to point out, is an association of all the municipalities of Canada for the purpose of protecting their rights. In the report of the secretary presented at their last annual convention in Ottawa in 1903, the report says :
Another subject of our labour has been the improvement of telephone legislation. During the session of 1902 the Minister of Justice had given his promise to introduce a General Telephone Bill which should contain some improvements in favour of our cause, the justice of which he admitted. As the work did not seem to proceed after a certain point, in the autumn, the Executive requested an interview, and met him at Ottawa by appointment on the sixth of February last. A pretty full interview was had, in which we placed before him the ' wishes of the municipalities, set forth in the proceedings of the union, and particularly their desire to control their streets and local franchises. He promised attention to the mat- , ter, and when the session arrived nothing was j done. It became apparent that other in- j fluences had been working his desire to im-Mr. FITZPATRICK.
|
prove his General Telephone Bill of the previous year in such a manner as to make it acceptable to municipal authorities, the Executive of the Union took an active interest in assisting in the improvement of the Bill of Mr. Maclean. A special sub-committee of the Railway Committee was formed, and numerous meet-i ings were held. The hostile influence, however, appeared to affect the operations of the special committee, and delays were systematically raised, which made it in the end self-evident that no real progress was desired by some of the members. It will be for this convention to inquire into the reasons of the course thus pursued, and to take such action as may seem proper.
That is the intention of this reference, to send the Bill to the Railway Committee for the Railway Committee to send it to a subcommittee for the purpose of getting all the information and once there the same thing will happen to this Bill as happened to the telephone Bill and no progress will be made, whereas if we can get this Bill in a committee of the House and it can be discussed in all its phases, the telephone question discussed by itself, both sides be heard, and every member given an opportunity to make a proposal himself and forced to vote and go upon record, we will get results of the kind desired. In shifting it over to the Railway Committee and treating it as the Telephone Bill was treated before, by a special committee, it will be hung up there and members wall not be compelled to vote on this question and yet it is a question in which the country is interested and on which it desires to know the record of members. I am not satisfied and I intend* to divide the House on this reference. I therefore move in amendment:
That the Bill be not referred to the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph lines, but that it be referred to a Committee of the Whole House.

I did not intend to take part in the discussion of this question, but it strikes me that we are hardly in possession of the information which would enable us to arrive at a correct conclusion. We are .none of us here representing a railway or any railway interest ; we are here representing only one side of a bargain. Every person in this House is interested in bringing down railway rates and the other side have not an opportunity of presenting their view of the case. It can be readily conceived that were one hundred consumers of flour to assemble themselves together and say what is the price of a barrel of flour it might not suit the millers. We must say : For years you have been getting $5 a barrel for flour, and we think it is time now that we one hundred oonsumers should buy it for $4 a barrel. But the miller would say :	You must take into consideration
what I pay for wheat and wages ; I am not able to reduce my price. There is not one gentleman in this House prepared to put himself in the position of the other man

who is a partner to this bargain. It is the ( easiest thing in the world for men who | have any interest at stake to legislate and j regulate concerns so that it will inure ulti- | mately to their benefit without considering how it will affect the other side of the transaction. Luckily in this country this question is relegated to the Dominion House. Speaking of the conditions on the other side of the line, where the individual states have the power, a writer recently has said :
At present it is the ambition and endeavour of each state to secure rates no higher-and perhaps a little lower,-than its neighbour. Kansas sees no reason why it should not have as favourable rates as Missouri or Indiana ; Missouri and Indiana will not tolerate any disadvantage as compared with Ohio, Ohio insists on equality with Pehsylvania and Massachusetts. Viewed by itself, the ambition of each individual state is intelligible and even praiseworthy ; but the net result in practice is intolerable injustice to the railways of the more sparsely settled sections.
The recent decision of the Supreme Court will go a long way toward protecting the companies against this injustice.
Briefly, what the Supreme Court says is that a state legislature has no right to impose any rates for the carrying of freight or passengers which are not high enough to produce a ' fair return ' on the ' fair value ' of the property of the railway companies ; also that the question whether any given rates are adequate or not is not a matter which a legislature can decide, but must ultimately be a subject of judicial inquiry.
It presupposes at once that the legislature is not trained in the consideration of railway questions that has only a selfish interest, as it were, in one side of this question, and that it is not possessed of the judicial functions necessary to a settlement of this question - fairly upon its merits. We, tonight in this House, represent only one side of the question and because the constituents of the hon. member for Lincoln say that they would like a two cent rate is no reason at all why a two cent rate shall be adopted by the railways. I would ask any hon. gentleman in this House, taking the railways in their concrete form with an invested capital of a thousand million of dollars and an earning power of only two and a half per cent, if we were by our act to reduce this revenue of two and a half per cent we would be dealing justly with the railways. Would it not be a fair proposition to take each individual railway and see whether it could stand a reduction ? If we did so we would find that scores of railways in Canada to-day are not earning one cent and if we took such action we would be making their investments still more profitless than they are. I shall, of course, support the resolution that has been moved that it shall go to the committee so as to give the people who are interested in seeing that the railways get justice an opportunity of presenting their case. We have a per-
, sonal and selfish end in reducing the rate j from three cents to two cents a mile. It i would add to our comfort and add to our | pecuniary advantage. We have two parties to the transaction ; one of them is precluded from expressing his views on the question and under those circumstances an injustice will be done.
We could very well conceive that where an employer of labour has power to dictate the terms under which he shall employ a man and shall say that $1.23 is his opinion as to the value of a day's work and that man has no recourse, $1.25 will be the reward of that man's day's labour, but it is not right to the labour mail. Neither is it right for us to say here without a tittle of information or experience and without taking into consideration the accommodation that is provided or what it costs the railway company that- 2 cents a mile is a proper rate to charge. Under these circumstances I am prepared to support the resolution that the question shall go on to the committee so as to give the railway companies an opportunity of presenting their case and see whether they would be justly treated by an arrangement like this.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to say anything on this question to-night or to take up the time of the House as there are so many other matters to be considered, but as it is to be pressed to an issue, I do not wish to give a silent vote in connection with the matter. There are some portions of the Bill which have my approval. I am not quite certain that I am ready to move for all that is contained in the Bill, but there is no question to my mind but what the express companies should be placed under the supervision of the Railway Commission. Their rates should be regulated. Any of us who have to do business with express companies know exactly how these companies use us when we have to pay what we consider excessive charges on small parcels. The business of express carriage is a large and growing trade, and a trade which is much easier to regulate now than it will be ten years hence. We will be able to regulate it now much more easier than we will be in the future. Then, the clause relating to telephones may not be drawn nroperly or it may interfere, as my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) has stated, with some case which is now pending before the courts, but there is no question in my mind but that telephones should have as free access to the railways of this country as possible and that the connection with telephones all over the country should be as free as possible having a certain regard for justice to all interests. In regard to the two cent rate we have all been thinking about that a good deal. The question of a maximum rate of two cents a mile upon the railways is a live question in the province of Ontario to-day, but I con-

I'ess myself, tliat I have not sufficient data or information to enable me to decide upon the matter. The reduction of the rate from three to two cents a mile is a bold step. It is a reduction of thirty-three and a third per cent in the earnings of the railways and while it may he in the interest of the people to make this reduction we may be injuring the railways in doing so. Let us endeavour to have sufficient information before us to enable us to make up our minds in connection with the matter intelligently. That is my view of the matter and under the circumstances, not having sufficient information at my command I feel disposed to allow this matter to go before the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph lines. I have no doubt hut that the whole question will come back to the House again this session and that we shall have ample opportunity to discuss it when we shall have sufficient information in regard to it. I thought before I looked up the public records that the railways of the' country earned more money than they do. The hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) stated that the railways in Michigan earning $2,000 a mile give a two and a half cent a mile rate and that those earning $2,500 a mile give a two cent rate	.
Those earning $2,000 a mile give a two and a half cent rate and those earning $2,500 a mile give a two cent rate.

The Canadian Pacific Railway's earnings last year were $1,460 per mile oil its road from passenger traffic. You see that is under the earnings of a road giving a two and a half cent rate. The Canada Southern earned $3,150 per mile. That is the best earning road we have in Canada. The Grand Trunk earned $2,200 a mile. Upon these figures the Canada Southern would come under the two cent rate, the Grand Trunk the two and a half cent rate and the Canadian Pacific Railway would still continue its three cent rate.
| Until we have obtained tlie information and until we have had the parties who are to be affected by a drop of thirty-three and a third per cent in their earnings before the committee so that they may have ail opportunity of placing their case before us we cannot intelligently decide whether this is a step which we should take or not. These are my views. I am prepared to support the resolution that the question be sent to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph lines.
The Minister of Justice moves that the Bill be referred to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.
I will withdraw my amendment so that we can divide on the main motion.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that he withdraws the amendment ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As evidence of the wisdom of my suggestion that this should be referred to the Railway Committee, I would like to read to the House a statement of what the law really is in New York and Michigan.
The law as to the state oi New York is stated by Mr. Henry Apthorp, of Cleveland, as follows :-
The statutes of New York permit generally, a three-cent rate, although a much higher rate is allowed on hilly roads.^ The two-cent law in New York which is the exception referred to and which has been the foundation of many and oft repeated arguments, applies only to way passengers on one part of one road, viz., to that part of the New York Central Hudson River Railroad which lies between Buffalo and Albany. Under the statute the fare is limited to two cents per mile from any intermediate stations to Albany, or from any intermediate station to Buffalo, or from any one intermediate station to another between Albany and Buffalo.
It does not apply to the fare from Albany station to Buffalo station, nor from Buffalo station to Albany station. It applies to local fares only between these two cities ; and not only does the law authorize more than two cents, hut three cents is the ordinary fare in force upon many of the railways in New York State as Mr. Apthorp shows, giving the following instances.
The fare on the Nickel Plate Railroad between Dunkirk and Buffalo, is $1.15 ; distance, 40 miles ; rate per mile 2-87 cents.
On the Brie Road from Elmira to Binghamp-ton, $1.70 ; distance, 57 miles ; rate per mile, 3 cents.
From Syracuse to Ogdensburgh on the New York Central the fare is $4.14 ; distance, 137 miles ; rate per mile, 3 cents.
From Syracuse to Watertown on the New York Central the fare is $2.25 ; distance, 73 miles ; rate per mile, 3 cents.
From Utica to Malone, New York Central Railroad, the fare is $5.01 ; distance, 167 miles; rate per mile, 3 cents.
Is the fare from Buffalo to Albany more than two cents ?

speechtext: At all events it is quite evident that there is conflict of opinion, to put it mildly, with respect to the facts.
