If we are in earnest and desire to ime pose a two-cent rate on all railways in Canada, surely the least the railway companies ought to expect is that they should have an opportunity to be heard. That is a matter of common justice. If these figures are correct they tell a different tale.
Who is the author of that book ? 1

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know.
Mi-. CLARKE, Is there anybody's name attached to it.
It blew into the House.
Will the Minister of Justice be good enough to hand that book over ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course. The quotations are said to be taken from page 699 of Poor's Manual, which is a well known authority. The average rate on the Grand Trunk Railway per passenger per mile is 1-78 cents and on the Canadian Pacific Railway 1-8 cents. Of course I do not know anything about these figures but assuming they are correct, you see at a glance what it would be to apply to the railroads in Canada, with their enormous mileage and sparsely settled country, the conditions that



prevail in these thickly settled parts of the United States. In any event, all that I suggest to the House is the propriety of further inquiry.

As I understand, all that xny hon. friend from East York desired was that similar consideration should he given to his Bill as was given to the Bill of my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster). He asked that the House should resolve itself into committee to consider the Bill, and he was willing that it should be afterwards referred to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not so understand him, and I think my hon. friend will agree with me that it would be a waste of time to go over all the figures here when we could have the matter much more conveniently dealt with in the Railway Committee.

I believe I am in error as to the position my hon. friend took, but I think the time occupied in a discussion of this measure here would not be time wasted. A good deal of information could be obtained from the hon. gentleman and others who have made a study of this question. I certainly laboured under the delusion that a two-cent rate prevailed throughout the state of Michigan and the state of New York ; for from the extracts read from the pamphlet by the Minister of Justice, which we are bound to accept, and which I understand are quotations from the statutes of both states, it appears that there is no fixed rule in that respect. I certainly think the matter is one that ought to be thoroughly investigated, and I should not desire to see my hon. friend's proposition treated as was his proposition of last year with regard to telephones. I happened to be a member of the sub-committee to which that measure was referred, and it was utterly impossible for us to get along. The matter was practically tied up. If the hon. minister will give us an assurance that an opportunity will be afforded to discuss the matter fully in the Railway Committee, I shall vote with him to have the Bill referred to that committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There can be no possible objection to that. The matter will be fully discussed in the Railway Committee and a decision come to there upon it ?
What I mean is that there shall be no reference of it to a sub-committee where it will be killed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that no such move will be made with a view of side-tracking the measure; but if the Railway Committee should think that it would advance the inquiry better by referring it to a sub-committee, it would be difficult for us to decide here that the committee shall not take that course.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: It would be a public inquiry which could be better conducted in the Railway Committee, where the majority of the members of this House could take part in it, and I would be prepared to support the motion of my hon. friend if the assurance were given us that we should have a free and full discussion of the measure in the Railway Committee.

The Minister of Justice, in giving the figures with regard to the state of Michigan, omitted to mention that for five miles or less the rate per mile is three cents. I understood that the hon. member for East York, in introducing his Bill, had two or three suggestions. One was a sliding scale, and another was a geographical arrangement; and he was willing to leave to the Committee of the Whole House the decision of what the rates should be. Taking that view, I supported the hon. gentleman in his proposition. A great deal has been said about the rates in the state of Michigan and the state of New York. Any one who'knows anything about railway matters in those states knows that south of Lake Erie a certain rate prevails in a certain area, and all the railways are governed by that rate. So it is in Canada north of Lake Erie. If the hon. gentleman makes a proposition reducing the rates to what would be fair and just, and applying the same rates to all railways on the same basis of income, I would be prepared to support him. There should be an exception where the earnings of one road are less than those of another.

I may say that the author of this pamphlet which the hon. Minister of Justice quoted, and the name of the author of which he had some difficulty in finding out, is Mr. Chrysler of this city, a man we often meet as a lawyer. There should uot have been great difficulty in ascertaining who the author of this valuable document is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The references I made were to Poor's Manual and to the statutes, and I was careful to guard myself by saying that I did not know who the author of the pamphlet was. It was handed to me by the Solicitor General, and I handed it to the hon. gentleman who I thought could read it and find out the author for himself.
Surely no person suggests that Mr. Chrysler garbled the extracts from Poor's Manual.

I would ask the hon. gentleman to give us the assurance that this Bill, if referred to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph lines, will be discussed and the evidence taken before the whole committee. If that assurance is given, I will vote for the proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend will not misunderstand me. I stated that

there was no desire on the part of the government to adopt the policy of appointing a sub-committee to side-track the measure ? but if the Railway Committee come to the conclusion that any good purpose can be served by appointing a sub-committee, I do not think we are in a position to guarantee that the Railway Committee shall not take that course.

As the government has control of the Railway Committee as well as the other committees, I think we will have to trust to its honesty of purpose and desire to have the question fully discussed in that committee and accept its proposition. I would therefore suggest to my hon. friend from East York that it is scarcely worth while dividing the House if the government only desire to bring out information which can be brought out before the Railway Committee, but could not before the Committee of the Whole House. He should however give us the assurance that the government will not allow the telephone and railway lawyers to take up the whole time of the committee from day to day and thus prevent the taking of any action.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. RALPH SMITH (Vancouver) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 35) respecting union labels. He said: I do not think it necessary, Mr. Speaker, to take up the :time of the House for many minutes in explaining this measure. A Bill similar to this has already gone through the House but was defeated in the Senate. This House has given its opinion three different times that the request made by the trades unions of this country in favour of a registration of the union label should be complied with. Members of this House on both sides have agreed to that principle, but unfortunately the Senate has seen fit to kill each Bill to that effect as it came before that body. The principle of the present Bill is very simple. It provides that any body of men may present a label representing their production to the Minister of Agriculture, and the Department of Agriculture shall provide a certificate of the registration of such label.
Could there be any objection to that ?

The House of Commons has never objected, but the objection comes from the Senate, inspired by the Manufacturer's Association. The union label is operating in this country very extensively, and there is nothing in this Bill which would bring about a condition of things that might not happen under the present operation of the label.

The use of the label is not compulsory ?
121$

No, there is nothing provided in the Bill to compel any employer to use it. The use of the label, if the Bill passes, will be the same as it is now. Tt will only become operative on the voluntary consent of the workingmen and the manufacturers. The Bill provides against a fraudulent use of the label. The request is a very reasonable one, and one which has been granted by thirty-one states of the American Union. Of course there the power to provide legislation of this kind is in the hands of the state governments, which is not the case in the Dominion, but thirty-one American states have provided for the simple principle of registration of the union label. In England the same thing is provided for under the Trade Marks Act and the Manufacturer's Association of that country do everything to encourage the operation of the principle of the label. In my opinion the tendency of the operation and use of this label would be to bring the organized bodies of workingmen and the organized bodies of manufacturers together and thereby bring about a better understanding between tlfem and better conditions of industrial peace. The remainder of the Bill consists simply of provisions for putting this principle into effect. The object is that upon the application of workingmen, the minister shall provide for the registration of every label. I therefore move the second reading.

I regret exceedingly that the rules of the House do not allow me to put the hon. gentleman's motion. The Bill is one which relates to and provides for imposing penalties in restriction of trade. By subsection (b) of section 6 it provides that it shall be lawful for any person, firm, labour union, &c., other than the labour union registering such label, unless with the consent of such labour union, to knowingly sell, offer for sale, or dispose of any article marked with such label or any part thereof ; or to counterfeit or imitate any such label; or to sell, offer for sale or dispose or in any way utter or circulate any counterfeits or imitation of any such label.
It is clearly in restraint of trade and must be introduced by resolution.

The rule is quite plain, and I need only quote it to prove to the House that the motion cannot be put. Rule 41 provides :
No Bill relating to trade, or the alteration, of the laws concerning trade is to he brought into this House, until the proposition has first been considered in a committee of the whole House and agreed unto by the House.
That means that there should be first a resolution?

Precisely. I find also at page 641, Bourinot:

In the Canadian House it is the practice to consider all fees and charges which go into the treasury in a committee , of the whole.
This Bill provides for fees for registration and the issue of certificates, and for that reason also I do not think that jthe second reading can be proceeded with. 1 an: inclined to believe that the Bill is also contrary to section 54 of the British North Aemrica Act, which provides :
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or Bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that House bv message of the Governor General in the session in which sgch vote, resolution, address or Bill is proposed.	.
I am not giving a rule on this last point, but am prepared to rule that because the matter is one which relates to trade, and because it has been our practice to deal with matters of this kind in committee and upon resolutions, I cannot allow this motion for the second reading to be put.
What course then, should the hon. member take 1
The course that is open to any member. Let him give notice of a resolution which will go on the order paper and be taken up in due course.
I shall provide the clerk with a notice to that effect.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ralph Smith) if this Bill is exactly on the same line as the one introduced before ?
I think it is the same, except that previously it was associated with the Trade Marks Act. This is an independent Bill for the union label.
Who prepared this Bill ?
I think this Bill was prepared by the lawyer of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, Mr. O'Don-oghue.

Mr. HAUGHTON LENNOX (South Sim-coe) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 13) to amend the Railway Act. He said [DOT] This is a matter that I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) will recognize requires rather careful handling. It is a matter that we had under discussion last session, and some of the ablest lawyers we had in the House at the time, including the Minister of Justice and Hon. Mr. Blair, then Minister of Railways, expressed opinions upon it. The object of the Bill is to prevent the railway companies contracting themselves out of their ordinary liability for negligence; that is such liability as at-

taches to them according to the law of the province in which they are operating. The Bill that I have introduced differs materially in structure from the Bill introduced by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) last year, and I believe it differs in principle as well. From a careful consideration of the matter I am led to believe that, even though it be true that the Bill of last year might offend against the principles which divide the jurisdiction of the Dominion parliament from that of the provincial legislatures, yet I think that, should that turn out to be the case the Bill I have framed does not offend in that regard. The railways chiefly pointed to by the Bill are the Grand Trunk and the Intercolonial Railway. The government, or the country, is unfortunately, in the same position, as regards what I consider the injustice to railway employees, as the Grand Trunk Railway itself. The example is spreading, and we see that the Algoma Central Railway Company are adopting the same policy, namely, under the guise of affording a benefit to their employees, holding out terms of insurance to them and of protection to their families after death of the bread-winner, robbing the families of the compensation they could have for the wrong, and very often the flagrant wrong of the railway companies.
I pause as the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) has made a suggestion to me as to proceeding further. I do not want, by any possibility, to lose the opportunity of dealling with this matter. Of course, I recognize that it is pretty late, and we do not wish to stay here unnecessarily. But I wish to discuss this matter and have it to go to the committee if possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) wishes to proceed, we have no objection. But, if it suits his purpose as well, to withdraw his motion and let the order stand in its place on the paper to be discussed at a future time we will call the day's work ended.

I think I had better proceed, but I will be as brief as possible. T have a word or two to say as to the origin of the difficulty in this case a very important point. I will ask the Minister of Justice to take this point carefully into consideration, as I know that what I have to address myself to more particularly is to satisfy the Minister of Justice that this does not conflict with the jurisdiction of the local legislature. I point out that the origin of the difficulty in this ease, the whole cause of the trouble, is the Act of 1874 and the Act of 1878 enacted by this parliament. The Act of 1874 was a kind of omnibus Act, and I venture to say was not appreciated by the members of the House at the time when it was passed. It provided for the consolidation of the debt of a railway, the rising of capi-

tail, the providing of a superannuation and provident fund and other things, and, in that way, I am disposed to think, it slipped through without it being appreciated that it was a disability and a danger to railway employees. In fact, I think there is abundant evidence to establish that at the time it was enacted not even the railway lawyers themselves appreciated the gravity of the Act or the use it could be put to. But in recent years we have had reason to see in this Act a means of depriving the families of railway employees of such poor consolation as they could get from the recovery of damages for the death of those upon whom they had depended. I will merely refer to these sections, and proceed to another branch of the - case. The difficulty culminated when the railway company, under powers granted by these statutes, passed their by-law No. 15, providing that:
(15.) In consideration of the subscription of the Grand Trunk Railway to the society, thereafter no member or his representative was to have any claim against the company for compensation on account of injury or death through accident.
Then rule 5 provides for membership in the company, and makes it compulsory upon the employees, with one or two exceptions, not of importance now, to become members of the insurance. In other words, what is practically and effectually, according to the decision of the court, a contracting-out clause. And let me say in passing-because it has been used as argument against the employees that they accepted the rules and by-laws and made no objection to .them, and paid under the regulations prescribed by the company-that although there is a pretty full index of the by-laws, yet there is no index pointing to the fact that there is such a clause as the one I have just referred to. I have now dealt with the provisions of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I shall presently refer to the use they make of the statutes they obtained from parliament in 1874 and 1878, and the effectual way in which they have used the clauses to which 1 have referred. It would surprise many members of the House-it certainly surprised me-to find that the Dominion parliament have adopted the same rule in reference to the Intercolonial Railway that has been adopted by the Grand Trunk.
Now I am here to say that I do not care how it cuts politically, I do not care who originated that clause, it is a most unfair and unjust provision by the'government on behalf of the people of Canada as against the employees of the Intercolonial. The significance of that and how it answers my purpose to refer to it, will appear pretty conclusively later on. The remedy that I propose for this difficulty is contained in a Ball which I shall not read at present, but the lines of which I wish to particularly impress upon the Minister of Justice. I am not asking to create any new
rights in the employees of the Grand Trunk Railway; I am not asking to interfere in any way with the rights of the people of any province as controlled by their legislature. What I seek by the Act is to leave the laws in these various provinces as they are and therefore to put beyond possibility any conflict with the provisions of section 92 of the British North America Act which conferred the rights on the provinces as contrasted with section 91 which defines the rights and jurisdiction of the Dominion parliament. I am not invading any rights, but I am endeavouring to do away with the effect of the invasion of the rights of the provinces effected by the statutes of 1874, and 1878, and to restore to the provinces the rights which they had up to that time.
Standing for provincial rights.

Standing for provincial rights incidentally. I am glad I do not invade provincial rights, but I am proceeding with the intention, mainly of standing for the rights of the employees of the Railway Committee, people who have not the means of going from court to court to assert their rights and so by appealing to a court of last resort obtaining that justice which the Minister of Justice said last year they would obtain if they carried their grievances to the court of highest appeal. If the Bill which I have introduced is passed it will simply prevent the railway companies, operating under Dominion charters, who have provided an insurance branch to their business, from setting up as a plea the fact that these parties have become members of an insurance company and so have disentitled themselves and their families in case of death to the ordinary compensation to which they would be entitled according to the laws of the province in which they live.
It will be evident if we refer to the cases which have been decided and which have caused attention to be brought to the evil that exists in this matter that I am right in saying that the whole difficulty arises out of Dominion legislation, and out of the fact that the statutes of the Dominion so control the statutes of the only provinces where these questions have yet arisen that it is impossible now in the face of the Dominion statutes for these people to get redress. So far as I am aware the only provinces in which this difficulty has distinctly come to an issue are the provinces of Quebec and Ontario and in these provinces these difficulties would not and could not have arisen if the provincial laws had been allowed to take their course.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In what way ? Would my hon. friend enlarge upon that point ?

In this way : Holden vs. the Grand Trunk, Harrison vs. the Grand

Trunk in the province of Ontario, and Grenier vs. the Queen and Miller vs. the Grand Trunk Railway in the province of Quebec, could not have been decided and would not have been decided against the plaintiff but for the existence of the statutes of which I am complaining and of which I wish to have such an amendment as will give these people the benefit of the ordinary laws of the province in which they live. Holden and the Grand Trunk was tried at Hamilton before Mr. Justice Falconbridge and a jury. There was of course a plea of contributory negligence and that plea was left for the decision of the jury, but there was also raised the question pleaded upon the record that the plaintiff, the widow of the deceased, was barred by reason of this rule No. 15 which I have read. The jury decided in favour of the plaintiff, that is, that the plaintiff was entitled to recover so far as the portion of the case committed to them was concerned, but Judge Falconbridge decided that this plea was a good plea and was an absolute bar to recovery by the plaintiff. The matter came up subsequently by way of appeal in Toronto and it was then decided by the judges of the divisional court that so far as the branch of the case tried by the jury was concerned the rights were with the defendants, the Grand Trunk, and that having been decided by the court they decided not to deal with the other questions, and left it in the position in which Judge Falconbridge had left it. Judge Falconbridge decided that so far as rule 15 was concerned, the plaintiff could not succeed, In the appeal court the plaintiff failed upon the other branch of the case and it was not necessary to consider the branch of the case which had been decided by Judge Falconbridge, and therefore the decision of Judge Falconbridge stands in Ontario as a decision to govern Ontario until it comes to a higher court.
Last year when this matter was before the committee of the whole House, Hon. Mr. Blair, the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, said :
I have no doubt that the hon. Minister of Justice is entirely right. You might as well say that because this parliament incorporates a company to carry on a wholesale dry goods business in the city of Toronto, all the relations between the employees and employers come within the legislative control of this parliament we have the right to say what the conditions of employment shall be. My hon. friend says that some judges have passed an opinion to that effect. I would like to see the case, because I can hardly realize that any judge of eminence in Ontario, could come to such a judicial determination.
Chief Justice Falconbridge is regarded by some hon gentlemen on this side of the House and by many hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House as an eminent jurist. Chief Justice Falconbridge is well known, particularly well known of late Mr. LENNOX.
years, and I think I can commend him as an eminent judge. But, if something more is required to show how a really eminent judge has decided the matter I will refer to the case of Harris and the Grand Trunk Railway Company decided on 11th January last and reported in 3 O. W. R. page 212. This report is in the same words as the case is reported in the ' Globe.' The ' Globe,' of 11th January, says :
The judge, without the aid of the jury, undertook (by consent of the parties) to determine an issue raised by the defence, that plaintiff was a member of the Grand Trunk Railway insurance and provident society, and by one of the rules of that society no member shall have any claim against the railway company for compensation on account of injury or death from accident. Plaintiff received $39 from the funds of the society. Held, following the decision of Falconbridge, C.J., in Holden vs. Grand Trunk Railway Company (decided in appeal upon other grounds, 2 O.W.R. 80) thaj this was a good defence to the action. Action dismissed without costs.
I was saying that this judge for eminence and ability would commend himself to the judgment of my hon. friends opposite, the decision is by Mr. Justice Britton. These are the Ontario cases and they are decided upon the ground that this rule exists and this rule as recited by the acts of incorporation of this company could not exist but for the Acts of 1874 and 1878 of this parliament. In the province of Quebec I refer to the case of Grenier vs. The Queen, and I remember that last year the hon. Minister of Justice reminded .us that he was engaged in this case and he also reminded us that a matter of representation arose. But, the decision of the case does not turn upon the question or representation; it was decided upon the ground of a contract such as that with which we are dealing. The chief justice says, at page 51, after referring to the fact that in the province of Quebec there is no such thing as a defence of common employment :
Therefore, unless the suppliant's husband had so contracted with the Crown as to relieve it from responsibility for his death by reason of the negligence of the servants of the Crown, the judgment in favour of the suppliant now under appeal ought to be maintained	That the action given by Art.
1056 C.C. is merely an embodiment in the Civil Code, of the action which had previously been given by the statute of Canada re-enacting Lord Campbell's Act is too plain to require any demonstration and nothing in the judgment of the judicial committee in Robinson v. Canadian Pacific Railway Company (1) controverts this proposition. It would follow, therefore, that the suppliant's husband by becoming a member of the Intercolonial Railway Relief and Assurance Association and thereby assenting to its rules and to the arrangement by which the Crown contributed $6,000 annually to the funds of the association, in consideration of which the association on behalf of its members renounced all claims against the Crown

which might arise from the injury or death of any of its members, -constituted a complete answer to the suppliant's petition.
After that he says, it must be acknowledged that such a contract is an effectual bar to suppliant's claim. So that although, as my hon. friend said last year, the other question was considered, the decision as is recognized in the judgment in Miller and the Grand Trunk Railway Company, turned upon the question that the husband of the plaintiff having contracted himself out of his right to compensation, the wife stands in no better position. The case of Miller vs. The Grand Trunk, the other case that has since been decided in the province of Quebec, was based upon the principle enunciated in Grenier vs. The Queen. So that, I think I can with very fair support claim, as I said a few moments ago, that but for the Act of the Dominion parliament this difficulty could not arise, and that we only require to allow free action to the laws of the various provinces ; and to say that although we allow the Intercolonial Railway to have an insurance company in connection with its undertaking and although we allow the Grand Trunk Railway Company to have such an association in connection with its undertaking or any other railway company, we will allow no railway company, incorporated by the Dominion parliament, and over which the Dominion parliament exercises jurisdiction, to have such rules and regulations framed under its statutes as will enable it to bar any employee from the relief or compensation which he would otherwise be entitled to according to the laws of the province because of the negligence of the railway company.
Now, I have not adopted last year's Bill for reasons which I have to some extent expressed already. I have endeavoured to frame this Bill upon other lines for other reasons as well. I wished to avoid as far as I possibly could the complication which rises from leaving preliminary questions to be decided by the judges. I wanted, as far as possible, to have the law so plaiD that no litigation could arise, so that the railway company will not be tempted to invite litigation because I recognize that when litigation arises in nine cases out of ten the family of the deceased railway employees must necessarily be the parties to suffer.
I would not attempt at this late hour to define the vexed and tedious question of just where the jurisdiction in various cases is; but I call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that the exceptions are very numerous, to the theory that this would be an invasion of property and civil rights within the definition of section 92 of the British North America Act. That section is subject, not only, to the important exceptions defined in section 91, but to the very significant exceptions in the body of section 92 as regards public works for the general advantage of Canada, and of course, railways for the general advantage of Canada. That is a broad and easy matter to follow, but what I want to call the attention of the minister to is, that when this parliament has authority over any specific subject, it is its duty to legislate for all matters which are reasonably incidental to or connected with that subject. If you-have, for instance, a transcontinental railway incorporated by the federal parliament, you have the right to legislate on every matter which is incidental to the carrying out of that undertaking as a whole, no matter how much it might otherwise infringe upon provincial rights. I see the Minister of Justice does not confirm that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We undoubtedly have the control over insurance, but would we have the right to make uniform clauses?

We would have the right to make uniform clauses. I do not see anything that suggests the contrary, The provincial legislatures have certain powers over a number of subjects, so long as they are not appropriated by the Dominion parliament. That has been decided in several important cases, both in the courts of Canada and in the Imperial Privy Council. If we incorporated an insurance company we would have complete control over all the matters that are incidental to that company. That does not prevent a local legislature supplementing that by providing that certain conditions shall also be complied with by every "insurance company doing business in the province. That was recognized when the question came up as to taxing banks and insurance companies. It was held by the Privy Council that the provinces could tax them on the basis of the revenue they derived, and also on their business premises. In other words, an organization cannot carry on business within a province without the license of the local legislature, and the local legislature can, by way of license or tax, impose conditions upon the carrying on of their business. In support of the proposition, that whatever matters are reasonably incidental to the carrying out of the undertaking are within the competence of the Dominion parliament. I refer to Levesque versus New Brunswick Railway Company (1899), This company was incorporated before confederation, and it was afterwards declared to be a railway company for the general advantage of Canada. The question came up as to the limit of the rights between the provincial and Dominion parliaments, and it was decided that the question of fencing being a matter which went to the question of the property located in the province, it was controlled by the provincial legislature; but as to the question of the time within which to bring the action, which is usualy regarded as a mat-

ter of procedure, and peculiarly within the power of the local legislature, it was decided that that was a matter within the competence of the Dominion parliament, as it was controlled by the Dominion Act. That has not been since questioned. I notice that statutes have been passed since on the same basis, and in the matter of the Audit Act, it was pointed out by Sir John Thompson in one of the amendments as being a matter which, upon that principle could be controlled by the Dominion parliament, although it was suggested by Sir Louis Davies that it could not. As to being reasonably incidental, I refer to in re the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the County of York. Burton C. J. said:-
In all matters affecting its construction, operation and management, everything in fact necessary to its full and efficient working, the legislation of 'the Dominion is of a paramount authority even though it intereferes with property and civil rights, and trenches upon matters assigned to the provincial legislature by section 92.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The best case on that point is Roy and the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Mr. LEN1VOX. There are a number of other cases, which I have here, but I need not cite them. The wording of this is peculiarly important in reference to what we are here dealing with. ' The operation and management of the railway and everything that is necessary for its full and efficient working ' surely would embrace the question of an insurance company as part of the organization. This shows clearly, I think, that the Dominion government have control in regard to a railway for the general advantage of Canada. In the case of Curran vs. The Grand Trunk Railway, where the Workmen's Compensation for Injuries Act of Ontario, limiting the damages, came in conflict with the Dominion Railway Act, section 289, where the damages are unlimited, it was held that the damages were not controlled by the Act of the Ontario legislature. It is a question of damages we are dealing with here, the railway company claiming that by reason of the Dominion enactment they are not liable to pay more damages than they would pay under the insurance branch. But the parliament which created this creature and gave it its rights can so modify and control these rights that it cannot set up that the insurance money should be compensation for the wrong it had done the person insured, he having paid in his lifetime for the insurance he gets. I was going to refer to a number of authorities in Privy Council cases; but as the hour is late, and as I know my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is familiar with all these cases, I will not trouble the House with them.
The position of the government with reference to the Intercolonial Railway I have referred to. I do not think it is a desirable position for the country to occupy. I wish it to be understood that I am not complaining of the attitude of the government itself. I am not saying that the blame belongs to this government. I have not concerned myself with that. For anything I know, this scheme may have been inaugurated under a former government. Whatever government has adopted this system, it is not to the credit of Canada that it should longer exist. I do not think it is fair or even honest to the employees of the Intercolonial Railway that it should be enforced in the future. In this connection-and I do it with the very greatest respect-I want to point the Minister of Justice to the position he occupies in this regard. Last year he told the House that the amendment then proposed could not be carried through, and that the law which had been declared by the Ontario judges was not correct. In other words, if it was carried sufficiently far, the decisions would be reversed. But let me ask the Minister of Justice how he can reconcile that statement with the fact that he defended on that ground. He put forward that very plea in the case of Grenier vs. The Queen, argued the case on that ground, and won it on that ground. How can he say for one moment that this is not the law ? I am quite aware that sometimes lawyers argue cases in which they are not quite sure they are right, in which they have a lingering doubt as to justice being on their side.
Has that any application to the present case ?

I do not think it has ; but I do not say that when we find the Minister of Justice representing the Dominion of Canada setting up that plea, it could not be possible that he then ^lad any doubt as to it being a correct statement of the law. In other words, we cannot conceive that the Minister of Justice defended that case and won that verdict from that woman who was bringing the action unless he believed it to be the law. Therefore, when my hon. friend said, a year ago, that it was not the law, I submit 'that for the moment he overlooked this circumstance; and if he will refresh his memory by reference to the case of Grenier vs. The Queen, in which he was engaged, he will see that the defence was pleaded as I say, argued as I say and decided as I say. Therefore, we can have no stronger ground than that the law in the case arising in the province of Quebec was then decided to be upon all fours with the decision of Mr. Justice Falconbridge and Mr. Justice Britton in the province of Ontario ; and, to make it stronger still, it is reafiirmed in the case of Miller vs. Grand Trunk Railway, decided on

the same authority, since we were discussing this matter a year ago.
Now, having regard to the large interests at stake, and to the fact that I am pleading, not for railway employees who are alive, but prospectively for those who have not the means of vindicating their rights in all the courts of the land, I have done all I could to familiarize myself with the matter and have drawn this amendment as carefully as possible. I can well anticipate that it might be an easy matter for the Minister of Justice, if he should so desire, to point out that in my limited experience it is not very well or artistically drawn. I am not greatly concerned as to whether it is technically correct or not.
I have discharged my duty when I have dene all I could to perfect this measure. Technicalities can be cured, and it is the duty of the Minister of Justice, as I believe it will be his pleasure, to correct any errors into which I may have fallen. I now leave the matter to him. It was the Dominion parliament which placed this difficulty in the way of these employees. I understand that there are 25,000 employees of the Grand Trunk Railway in Canada. The authority I have for this is the statement of the hon. gentleman who introduced the Bill last year. Assuming that to be correct, in this one railway company alone there are probably 100,000 people are dependent upon the righting of this grievance. The Intercolonial has adopted the same position and other railway companies are following in this wake. The Grand Trunk, by its new rules, is becoming more rigid and advancing further still. It is therefore high time for the government to take up the matter seriously and endeavour to right this grievance. Just one word as to a possible objection'. Last year I was asked whether I considered that a special Act could be amended by a general Act without mentioning it. I may say that we are having such general Acts every day. The other day, when it was proposed to have alien labour legislation in a special Act, we were told that we would have a general Act governing the Transcontinental and all other railways regarding alien labour. These general Acts are constantly passed affecting corporations and institutions all over the country, but if it be necessary to make special reference to the particular Act, let the Grand Trunk Railway be named. If necessary to make any amendments. I would ask the government to make them, and I submit, not as a matter of special favour, but of simple justice to people whose rights are invaded, without, I believe, parliament intending that the statutes would be put to the use it has been, that these amendments, if necessary, should be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is an interesting question which we had occasion to consider last session. I must say that up to the
piesent I have not been able to see any very good reason to depart from the opinion I expressed last year that the legislation is ultra vires. In view however of the further information we have had from the hon. gentleman, I would suggest that in order that I may be able to further consider the Imaitter, I should be allowed to move the adjournment of the debate.

In a question of such importance as this, we are entitled to expect from the Minister of Justice something more than the scant courtesy he is giving it now. He has had a long time to consider this matter. It has not been sprung upon him without notice. He knows it is an important matter, and to tell us now that he requires further time to consider it, is simply treating the measure in a way which its importance does not deserve. I would not pretend to argue the legal phase of the Bill, but there is one thing certain. That is that this parliament should correct the wrong that may have been done by legislation or by lack of legislation ; and to refuse to deal with a question so important as this, when the evils complained of are constantly growing greater, is>
certainly showing most reprehensible neglect. We have a large number of men employed in Canada by two railway corporations-the one under the control of the Crown and the other a private corporation. I might well repeat what was said by the hon. member for South Simcoe, namely, that it was not creditable to the parliament of Canada to have passed such legislation and afterwards allowed it ho remain of the statutes. No man who gives value in the shape of work for the money he is paid should by reason of any contribution by a government or corporation to any system of insurance, the premiums upon which he pays himself, be put under any obligation to any corporation by reason of such payments. Any contract with such conditions is immoral and should not be continued a single day, and I am surprised that the Minister of Justice should have set up the plea that he had not time to consider this measure. How long does he want to consider it, or does it mean that he does not consider the question worth his serious consideration '! I know he is a busy man. but that is not a sufficient excuse for having overlooked so important a question. Unless he is ready to give us the assurance that he will take up this matter during the present session and treat it as seriously as it deserves, I think it may be taken for granted that he is simply prepared to dig a grave for the Bill. I hope I am entirely wrong and that tue hon. gentleman will give us some assurance that this measure will be taken up during this session.

Perhaps the Minister of Justice would allow this House to pass the second reading without committing the gov-

etnment to the principle of the Bill. That would advance it a stage and next Monday the matter could be brought up again.- A large number of railway employees look upon this as a very serious question. The Minister of Justice by advancing the Bill 'a stage will show the employees generally that the government are not putting barriers in the way of this legislation.
Many years ago this matter was brought up in the Ontario legislature, and the employees of the railway were asked their opinions with respect to it. They decided by a large majority in favour of legislation which would protect them. It is a well-known fact that, a good employee in the' railway or any other service will always protect his family by insurance and in every other possible way. If an employee protects his family by insuring for all he can pay, is it not an injustice that the railway company should call upon him, as a condition of his being employed, to sign a document which contracts the company out of their liability for damages because of injury ? That is what the Grand Trunk does, and I am sorry to see the Intercolonial following the same course. This is a serious matter for these men, and it is a matter that has been before them for a great many years. I think the Minister of Justice should allow this Bill to advauce a stage, without committing himself, and before next Monday he can look into the matter and give a decided answer. I again press upon the government and especially upon the Minister of Justice the importance of this question to thousands and thousands of men. These men look upon this question in a more serious light than hon. gentlemen may be aware of.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Last session, when this matter came up in amendment to the Railway Act, I did consider it. I must say frankly to the House, that the point was not then considered by me for the first time. I was Solicitor General at the time when the case of Grenier vs. the Queen, to which the hon. gentleman has referred, came up, and I had to argue it from the government point of view before the Supreme Court. I admit that I thought the question closed so far as I was concerned, and that it was not necessary to consider it further. But I say in all seriousness that my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) has put it in a somewhat different light. I am so constituted that I cannot make up my mind at once on a point; I want time to consider; and what I ask is that the hon. gentleman should allow the ' matter to be deferred for further consideration. Of course, the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) suggests that I should be able to make up my mind at a glance. Well, I know what I think of men who make up their minds at a glance and who express their opinions off-hand, and I suppose if I should follow that course people would have the same Mr. INGRAM.
opinion about me. I want time to reflect. The object 1 have in view is to see whether, in view of the serious argument, the very able argument, of my hon. friend, I may not change my mind.

Would the hon. Minister (Mr. Fitzpatrick) see any objection to letting it stand, retaining its position? I presume that could be done, with the consent of the House. I certainly do not want to press it as though I did not fully believe in what the Minister of ^Justice has said. I understand, of course, that he is perfectly candid in what he says.
Motion (Mr. Fitzpatrick) agreed to, and debate adjourned.
FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved the adjournment of the House.
Can the minister (Mr. Fielding) say what business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Bills that stand on the order paper other than the Militia Bill. If we dispose of these, the House will resume in Committee of Supply, taking up the estimates of Inland Revenue, and, perhaps of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. There are also some special items of estimates which will have priority.
Motion agreed to and House adjourned at 12.20 a.m., Tuesday.
